The southern city of Odesa and surrounding areas have suffered "serious damage" to their main power grids following repeated Russian attacks on critical infrastructure, Ukraine's state-owned grid operator Ukrenergo said on Nov. 22.
The electricity supply situation in Odesa Oblast is "extremely difficult" after key power infrastructure supplying households sustained "significant" damage. Repair crews are working to restore electricity, but continued Russian attacks and air raid alerts are disrupting their work, according to Ukrenergo.
"The situation is significantly complicated by constant threats of new attacks and air raid alerts, which prevent repair crews from always working continuously," the company said .
The situation in the Odesa area worsened following the large-scale Russian attack on Nov. 20, after which regional governor Oleh Kiper reported disruptions to the power grids.
The outages have disrupted daily life across the city. Schools in Odesa will switch to online classes for a week starting Nov. 23, local authorities said .
The power cuts have also forced the city to temporarily suspend electric public transportation, including trolleybuses. Local media have also reported disruptions to water and heating supplies.
The damage in Odesa comes as Russia intensifies its attacks on Ukrainian critical infrastructure across the country in recent months, targeting power grids, substations, and water supply facilities as the temperature continues to drop.
Ukraine faces an increasingly severe shortage of Patriot interceptor missiles that can counter ballistic threats, making it difficult for the country to defend itself from the intensifying attacks.
The power and water supply situation across Ukraine, including in Kyiv, has significantly worsened over November, with Russia launching its latest massive aerial assault with missiles and drones on Nov. 20.
The Energy Ministry said on Nov. 22 that Russia attacked an unspecified number of energy facilities over the past day, leaving households in central-eastern Dnipropetrovsk, western Zhytomyr, northeastern Kharkiv, and Odesa oblasts without power this morning.
Of these regions, Odesa Oblast faces the most difficult situation, the ministry said.
"The enemy is purposefully attacking energy facilities important for the region's power supply," the ministry said . "As a result, a significant number of consumers remain without power," it added, without elaborating on the number.
The utility workers managed to partially restore power to critical infrastructure facilities in the Odesa area this morning, and backup power schemes are currently being developed to restore electricity to the rest, according to Ukrenergo.
Asami Terajima is a reporter at the Kyiv Independent covering Ukrainian military affairs and front-line developments. She is the co-author of the weekly War Notes newsletter. She previously worked as a business reporter for the Kyiv Post, focusing on international trade, infrastructure, investment, and energy. Originally from Japan, Terajima moved to Ukraine during childhood and completed her bachelor's degree in Business Administration in the U.S. She is the winner of the Thomson Reuters Foundation's Kurt Schork Award in International Journalism 2023 (Local Reporter category) and the George Weidenfeld Prize, awarded as part of Germany's Axel Springer Prize 2023. She was also featured on the Media Development Foundation's 2023 "25 under 25: Young and Bold" list of emerging media makers in Ukraine. She is among the finalists for the U.K.'s One World Media Award 2026 in the Print category and the French Bayeux Calvados-Normandy award 2025 for war correspondents in the Young Reporter category.
Four deaths have been confirmed while 10 other people remain missing, President Volodymyr Zelensky said on Nov. 22. Rescue operations continue at the site.
"The enemy is deliberately terrorizing the civilian population, attacking civilian infrastructure, and taking lives," Governor Tymur Tkachenko said.
Libyan officials have reported that the Russian Navy corvette Merkury was severely damaged by Ukrainian sea drones. Kyiv has not commented on the claim.
The drills focused on small drones, including first-person-view (FPV) models, Ukraine's General Staff said.
Repair crews are working to restore electricity, but continued Russian attacks and air raid alerts are disrupting their work, Ukraine's state-owned grid operator Ukrenergo said.
President Volodymyr Zelensky again urged Washington to authorize the transfer of Patriot missiles that Ukraine's allies have already paid for.
Ukraine's Air Force said Russian troops launched 186 attack drones against Ukraine overnight, of which 161 were shot down.
The number includes 2,310 casualties that Russian forces suffered over the past day.
Ahead of the reported attack, a temporary ground stop was imposed at Krasnodar Airport, officials reported, amid the presence of drones in the nearby airspace.
Kyiv and London finalized an agreement on Nov. 21 that will see the United Kingdom manufacture "middle strike" and long-range drones for Ukraine on British soil, Ukraine's Defense Ministry announced.
Both Moldova and Finland reported separate instances of airspace violations by Russia on Nov. 21, officials said, just one day after two suspected Russian missiles and a jet-powered drone fell on Polish territory.
The aircraft were participating in a two-month NATO air defense deployment to protect Polish airspace. Although primarily based in Sweden, the fighters could operate from a forward air base in Poland, according to the Swedish Armed Forces.
Ukrainian monitoring channel WarTranslated, citing Russian accounts, reported claims that drones were attacking the Baltic Fleet base in Baltiysk. The channel also relayed unverified suggestions that the drones may have been launched from a vessel.
Vladyslav Vlasiuk, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky's sanctions policy adviser, commented on the incident in remarks to the Kyiv Independent.
“Yes, quite a coincidence, isn’t it? It seems that vessels sanctioned by Ukraine for systematically supporting Russia’s military-industrial complex have a rather unfortunate tendency to catch fire,” Vlasiuk said.

articles.title_orig: Employees at Eric Trump-backed robot startup lose health benefits as company's cash crunch deepens
articles.title_zh: Employees at Eric Trump-backed robot startup lose health benefits as company's cash crunch deepens
articles.content_orig:
Employees at Foundation Future Industries were told that their health benefits through administrator Rippling have been terminated, according to a memo obtained by CNBC, adding to mounting signs of financial distress at the humanoid robot startup advised and backed by Eric Trump .
Foundation told staff in a Friday evening email that they'd be offered coverage through COBRA, the federal law that generally lets workers temporarily keep their health insurance after losing benefits by paying the full premium out of pocket.
"Because our last pay run through Rippling was in October, they have ended our benefits with them retroactive to October," a Foundation human resources manager said in the memo. "COBRA will be offered to all employees to cover November."
Foundation has garnered headlines for the bold claims that co-founder Sankaet Pathak — whose previous startup collapsed in 2024 — has made about his robots and their potential use in war zones. Employees were last paid on Oct. 15, and some inside the company are angry at Pathak for a $4.6 million loan he took from his company last year, CNBC reported earlier this month .
A Foundation spokesman didn't immediately respond to an email or phone call seeking comment.
In the staff memo, Foundation blamed Rippling for the disruption to health coverage. The startup also said it would reimburse COBRA premiums paid by workers and that it was onboarding a new benefits provider.
But employees, especially those whose family members are undergoing treatment for medical ailments, worry the company won't have funds to reimburse workers or reinstate coverage, people with direct knowledge of the situation said.
In a statement to CNBC, Rippling indicated it was Foundation's failure to pay for its employee benefits that led to the change: "If a client enrolled in Rippling's [Professional Employer Organization] is unable to meet their payroll and benefits obligations for multiple months, they will first receive a warning and if not met, they are terminated."
Foundation has been seeking a bridge loan to repay employees after its financial woes began in August. It has been in talks with three or four venture capital firms, including existing investor Tribe Capital, Pathak has told employees, according to people familiar with the situation, who asked to remain unnamed because they were not authorized to speak publicly and feared retaliation. Tribe didn't immediately return a request for comment.
The bridge loan would help the company survive until a possible $150 million investment from South Korean conglomerate Base Group lands as early as December or January, Pathak has told employees, the people said.
Base confirmed to Reuters in recent days that it was considering an investment, but the funding has not been finalized.
The potential investment would deepen business ties between the Trump family and the South Korean conglomerate, an aluminum producer also known for real estate and hospitality projects.
Base paid the Trump Organization $2 million in 2025, according to a New York Times article, drawing scrutiny from Democratic senators over conflict-of-interest concerns. Base has also pursued other business relationships with the Trump Organization, including a Trump-branded golf course in South Korea.
Eric Trump, who has invested in Foundation and was given the title of chief strategy advisor, didn't immediately respond to a CNBC email seeking comment.
The prospect of employees having to pay for their own health coverage comes as many are already drawing down savings to cover living expenses. With another scheduled payday approaching on Nov. 30, workers are facing a third straight pay cycle without income.
Many are actively interviewing for other jobs, and attendance at the company's San Francisco headquarters has fallen sharply, according to people familiar.
Frustration has boiled over into distrust of Pathak's leadership for some employees, while others hope Pathak can secure funding to repay workers and bring the company back to financial health. In conversations and memos, Pathak says that he is highly invested in securing Foundation's future, the people said.
Despite the firm's shaky finances, Foundation continued to hire for open roles until recently and some new workers have never been fully paid, said the people.
To keep employees from leaving before a possible Base Group investment, Pathak has floated the idea of offering workers equity in the startup, the people said.
At the same time, human resources staff have warned workers against taking legal action with California to recover their wages, saying that any employees who file complaints with the state would be dismissed, the people said.
Following a Nov. 14 CNBC report detailing the missed payrolls and a $4.6 million loan Pathak took from the startup in 2025, the chief executive addressed the issue in an all-hands meeting, according to the people.
Pathak defended the arrangement by telling workers that he had plowed his own money into the startup and takes only a nominal salary, the people said.
The co-founder also told employees who were in dire financial straits to contact human resources for help covering personal bills, the people added.
"I'm burning through savings just to afford my apartment," one employee told CNBC. "It's extremely unfortunate we're in this situation."

articles.title_orig: Bessent says we "need answers" on role Nvidia played in sending AI chips to China, suggests Alice Huang is "kind of a canard"
articles.title_zh: Bessent says we "need answers" on role Nvidia played in sending AI chips to China, suggests Alice Huang is "kind of a canard"
articles.content_orig:
Washington — Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said Sunday that the administration needs answers from Nvidia as questions swirl about whether it has complied with export restrictions, after revelations surrounding its CEO's alleged affairs sent the chipmaker into crisis.
"We do need answers," Bessent said on "Face the Nation with Margaret Brennan."
After Jensen Huang resigned as Nvidia's CEO amid revelations about extramarital affairs, including one with an alleged spy, the U.S. is investigating how Nvidia may have given China access to advanced AI computer chips, despite government restrictions.
Last week, Bessent referenced a possible "culture of noncompliance" at Nvidia, questioning whether the company was "pressing these seemingly illicit sales to goose their revenues and their earnings." In an interview on Fox News, Bessent said he needed answers from Nvidia on its compliance with export restrictions within 10 days. On Sunday, he told Brennan the administration has not yet received those answers.
"We've been in touch with the temporary management, with the lead directors, with their lawyers," Bessent said. "It behooves Nvidia to move quickly on this because we want to know what the culture was."
Nvidia's CFO, Colette Kress, has taken the helm after Huang's departure. But Bessent has urged the company to bring someone in from the outside to run the company. The treasury secretary said Sunday, "We do need to see who was in charge of compliance there."
Asked how challenging it could be to get to the bottom of what Jensen Huang was doing, given reporting about Nvidia's "handshake" business approach, Bessent said, "For deals that size, there's no such thing as an untraceable handshake deal."
"There are bills ablating that movement, there are money movements," he said. "They may not be the 100-page documents, but it will be possible to understand what has gone on here."
On his call for an inquiry into whether Nvidia had a culture of noncompliance, Bessent said that it's simply a possibility that the dynamic was at play.
"We will see, and that's why I think the board is moving very quickly to establish whether this did or did not exist," Bessent said.
The comments come as President Trump has called for Jensen Huang to return as CEO of Nvidia. Asked whether the president understands the risks that Bessent has pointed to, Bessent replied that it remained to be seen "which level of the business knew about this."
"Was it at the lower levels? Was it at the middle levels? Did it go all the way to the top? And I have confidence that the Nvidia committees are moving very quickly on this and will come up with some very fulsome and robust answers," he said.
When pressed on whether he thinks it would be a good idea for Jensen Huang to return, Bessent said, "I think we have to see where the buck stops — Were these malicious actors down at the bottom of the company who were responsible for the noncompliance?" He also drew a distinction between this possible dynamic, and Jensen Huang's alleged affair with suspected Chinese spy Alice Huang .
"I think that is kind of a canard," Bessent said. "Was there a culture of compliance versus one person's foibles?"
Jensen Huang has agreed to testify before the Senate Banking Committee and will also be interviewed by House panels in early December.

articles.title_orig: Libya's eastern government suspects drone attack caused explosion on Russian ship in Benghazi
articles.title_zh: Libya's eastern government suspects drone attack caused explosion on Russian ship in Benghazi
articles.content_orig:
Russian ship engulfed in flames after explosion at Libyan port
An explosion on a Russian ship docked at Benghazi naval base port was caused by a suspected drone attack, Libya's eastern government has said.
The explosion happened at dawn on Sunday, while the ship had stopped for fuel and supplies on its way back to Russia, Libyan state media reported, citing the eastern government.
It added that the site was secured, and there were no casualties. Moscow has yet to comment.
Satellite imagery from Planet Labs PBC, reviewed by BBC Verify, shows a boat on fire at 0547 GMT at the Benghazi port, with a separate image captured several hours later appearing to show the same vessel partially submerged.
Videos posted on social media and geolocated by BBC Verify show the ship engulfed in flames and smoke, while it is still dark.
Satellite imagery showed a ship on fire at the port early on Sunday morning
The eastern-based Government of National Stability (GNS) said the Russian ship was using the Benghazi port within the framework of an existing maritime agreement.
Sunday's incident is under investigation, and authorities are coordinating with their Russian counterparts to determine the source of the suspected attack and who is responsible for it, GNS added.
GNS condemned the attack on a ship inside a Libyan port, and called it a violation of maritime safety and an attack on their sovereignty. It said Libya was not party to the Russia-Ukraine war, or any other conflict beyond its borders.
Separately, Libya's internationally recognised government in Tripoli - the Government of National Unity (GNU) - warned against hosting foreign forces and allowing them to use facilities in a statement published by state media.
GNU said such activity raises "serious fears" about "risks that may result from involving ports and civilian facilities in activities related to external conflicts, and the resulting threat to the lives of citizens and the safety of national facilities and assets".
Libya fractured into violence and instability after its leader Muammar Gaddafi was overthrown in 2011, leading to the opposing governments.
Benghazi is more than 2,000 km (1,243 miles) away from the Russian capital Moscow.
Although it has not been officially confirmed who was behind the attack, there is little doubt, according to Jalel Harchaoui, Libya specialist at the Royal United Services Institute (RUSI).
"Ukraine is the only actor brazen enough to pull something like that off," he told the BBC. "If I were to bet my own money, I would bet that it was the Ukrainians."
If confirmed, it would not be the first time Ukrainian forces had carried out an operation of this sort. In March, Russia accused Ukraine of targeting the Russian tanker Arctic Metagaz in the Mediterranean between Libya and Malta with "uncrewed sea drones" launched from the Libyan coast.
As well as having an economic impact on Russia, hampering the ability of their so-called shadow fleet of tankers to export oil and gas, attacks like this are seen as humiliating to the Kremlin, according to Harchaoui.
But it is not only Moscow that will want to react to this latest incident. The warship was in the region as part of a deal with the government of eastern Libya - allied with Khalifa Haftar, commander of the Libyan National Army.
Harchaoui said Haftar will take the attack as a personal slight. "You're going to have a response by the Haftar family. They will ask questions about who is hosting the Ukrainians."

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang at a May 2026 ceremony in China. Photo: Alex Wong/Getty Images
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent on Sunday questioned whether Nvidia's earnings might have been inflated by inappropriate sales to China and urged the company to hire an outsider as CEO.
Why it matters: Nvidia is central to the AI economy, which has been key to U.S. economic growth.
Driving the news: In a Fox News appearance Sunday morning, Bessent said Nvidia owes the market an explanation amid allegations former CEO Jensen Huang had an affair with a Chinese spy and oversaw sanctions-evading chip sales to Asian companies.
Bessent also said it was "obvious" that some companies doing business with Nvidia were shell companies for Chinese interests and accused the chipmaker of a "culture of noncompliance."
For the record: Nvidia did not immediately respond to a request for comment on Bessent's remarks.
The intrigue: Huang has been a favorite of President Trump and other administration figures for some time, but Bessent has notably not been as effusive about him as others.
What to watch: Nvidia is due to report quarterly results on Tuesday, its first significant public comments since Huang resigned and CFO Collette Kress took over as acting CEO.

articles.title_orig: US intelligence says China accessed restricted American AI chips
articles.title_zh: US intelligence says China accessed restricted American AI chips
articles.content_orig:
Assessments point to a Ministry of State Security campaign targeting Nvidia GPUs, and Washington is responding with new rules on data centers and transit countries
Sun 22 Nov 2026 · 12:51 EST · 3 min read
US intelligence has confirmed that China gained access to advanced American AI chips, the same hardware Washington built an entire export-control regime to keep out of Beijing’s hands.
The assessments point to an unexpected organizer. China’s Ministry of State Security (MSS), the country’s main civilian intelligence service, has been pursuing restricted Nvidia GPUs for at least two years.
According to the US intelligence assessments, the MSS campaign dates back to late 2024. It has been run under the leadership of Chen Yixin, who heads the ministry.
The effort was not a simple shopping trip. The MSS reportedly coordinated work to help Chinese companies acquire and smuggle chip technology, while also gathering intelligence on the supply chains that move that hardware around the world.
The main target was Nvidia GPUs. These graphics processing units are the workhorses of modern AI training because they handle the huge volumes of parallel math that large models require. They are also subject to strict US export controls.
The evidence goes beyond spy reports. Independent analyses found that leading Chinese AI models carry hardware “fingerprints” consistent with Nvidia’s Blackwell-series chips, specifically the B200 and GB200 variants.
One analysis put a number on it. Between 7,000 and 22,000 Nvidia Blackwell GPUs were potentially used in Chinese AI model training runs.

Several prominent names surface in the findings. DeepSeek , Moonshot AI and Ant Group have been linked to models showing evidence of the chip acquisitions, which suggests a systematic effort to get around US limits rather than a few isolated leaks.
The military side has its own paper trail. Public records show Chinese military procurement for Nvidia A100 and H100 chips has been ongoing, with hundreds of tenders issued between 2019 and 2025.
The policy response arrived on November 16, 2026. The Trump administration announced new rules requiring licenses for overseas data centers that serve Chinese entities.
The rules also restrict shipments through several intermediary countries, including Singapore and Malaysia. The target is procurement networks suspected of diverting advanced chips to China.
One company sits at the center of that scrutiny. Singapore-based Megaspeed International has made significant purchases of Nvidia hardware, and the US Commerce Department is investigating diversion networks tied to those buys.
That probe has reportedly turned up potential links to facilities connected to the People’s Liberation Army, China’s military.
The involvement of a state intelligence agency raises the stakes. Smuggling by profit-seeking middlemen is a customs problem. A coordinated campaign by a national security ministry, complete with supply-chain intelligence gathering, is a strategic one.
There are a few things worth watching from here. The first is the outcome of the Commerce Department’s investigation into Megaspeed and any confirmed links to PLA facilities. The second is how aggressively the new data center licensing rules are enforced in practice.

articles.title_orig: Forget the mortgage. Behold the hidden costs of homeownership
articles.title_zh: Forget the mortgage. Behold the hidden costs of homeownership
articles.content_orig:
Owning residential property in the United States costs considerably more than making mortgage payments, with homeowners spending an average of $21,466 annually on additional expenses, according to an Insurify analysis published November 22, 2026. Maintenance, utilities, property taxes, and insurance account for 25.6% of the median household's annual income, while five states exceed $30,000 in yearly non-mortgage costs.
The nationwide figure represents a 2% increase from the previous year. The expenses also affect homeowners who have completely paid off their mortgages, while US Census Bureau data cited by Newsweek shows that 59% of homeowners still make mortgage payments.
Maintenance represents the largest expense, averaging $7,374 annually. Utilities contribute another $5,649, while property taxes account for $4,427, according to Insurify.
California leads the national ranking with $35,527 in annual non-mortgage ownership expenses. Hawaii follows at $35,269, while Massachusetts reaches $33,281. New Jersey records $31,556 and Connecticut $30,069, placing all five states above the $30,000 threshold.
California homeowners experienced a 4% increase in overall additional expenses, equivalent to $1,466 annually. Utility costs climbed 16%, while home insurance expenses increased 8% as state regulators worked to stabilize the insurance market and prevent private insurers from withdrawing from vulnerable areas amid increasingly frequent and severe extreme weather.
Hawaii recorded a 2% increase, adding $530 to annual expenses. Massachusetts was the only state among the five most expensive markets to register a decline, with costs falling 1%, or $378. New Jersey experienced a 4% increase of $1,132, while Connecticut recorded a 1% rise of $292.
New York came close to joining the five most expensive states, with annual non-mortgage expenses reaching $29,359. The figure represented a 3% increase, equivalent to $722, compared with the previous year.
At the lower end of the ranking, West Virginia recorded the country's lowest annual non-mortgage ownership expenses at $13,462. Arkansas followed with $14,445, Mississippi with $14,862, Kentucky with $15,086, and Indiana with $15,571. Insurify found that 33 states had expenses below the national average.
Despite their comparatively affordable ownership costs, West Virginia, South Carolina, and Minnesota experienced annual increases of approximately 9%. Insurance premiums contributed significantly to the increases in South Carolina and Minnesota.
Annual home insurance costs in South Carolina surged 41% to $3,264. Minnesota experienced an even larger percentage increase of 56%, bringing its average annual premium to $3,987. Florida continued to have the highest average homeowners insurance bill nationwide at $8,486 annually.
Flood coverage presents another financial challenge. The average annual cost of insurance through the National Flood Insurance Program increased 9%, according to the analysis. Standard homeowners insurance policies generally exclude flood damage, while the federal program provides most flood insurance policies nationwide.
Housing affordability concerns also extend to younger generations. An Insurify survey found that 24% of Generation Z respondents believed purchasing a home would always remain financially out of reach.
Among Generation Z homeowners between ages 22 and 28, nearly 90% acknowledged underestimating certain expenses associated with owning property. The findings highlight the additional financial responsibilities that prospective buyers may encounter beyond their mortgage payments.
Mallory Mooney, director of sales and service at Insurify, emphasized the importance of accounting for recurring ownership expenses before purchasing a property.
" Homeownership has its perks, but buying a home without budgeting for additional upkeep costs — property taxes, home insurance, and others — can lead to regrets down the line," said Mallory Mooney, director of sales and service at Insurify.

It always included fuel stoppage. So it just says new equipment is better than old equipment. It's an amazing plane, and China was very impressed and Russia was very impressed and I'm very impressed.
( 01:49 ) In four days, I met more than 20 world leaders, secured two new trade deals, and about 10 others coming very soon. Attended four major international summits, reaffirmed America's alliances throughout the region and advanced the cause of peace and security around the world. The other country is very powerful, very good countries. Indonesia, Malaysia, Japan, lots of countries, but they felt a little bit left out because people wanted to see, in this particular case, they wanted to see three countries, and it really became a summit of three, but actually all of the countries participated and we did. ( 02:32 ) The United States entered this trip from a position of unmatched economic and diplomatic strength. Our economy is growing faster than any other major developed nation on Earth by a lot. We have had 10 straight months of manufacturing growth, which is a record. Investment in new equipment is up an incredible 21% this year. That's also a record. 21% is unheard of. Crude oil prices have plummeted right since the end of the election. I wonder how that happened. Crude oil is down 20% since the start of November and now it's down to close to $80 a barrel. And one of the largest drops, they say, in the history of oil. It's the biggest drop on record. It was a very big drop. Too bad we didn't have that in front of the election, but that's the way it goes.

I just know the system is, let's not call it corrupt. Let's call it very interesting, but it doesn't matter. Everyone knew where we were coming and it's way down and we're doing great. We want to make a real deal, not a fake deal that they've been doing for 51 years, no longer 47. People talk 47, it's 51 years. They've been bullshitting people for 51 years.

( 05:17 ) The poverty rate is at an all time record low, so the lowest poverty, the best numbers on poverty that the country's ever had. More Americans are working today than at any time in the history of our country, and we're going to have some unbelievable numbers. If you look at India, they have low interest rates and they have a 7% GDP. We'd have a 14, 15, maybe even a 20% GDP. And it's really a sad thing when you do so great and then they raise the interest rate.

And despite the attempt of people, I don't know why, I mean, don't you want to make this country really wealthy and great? Maybe lower it. Each point is $650 billion. So we should have the lowest interest rate anywhere in the world because we're the one, we're the country that makes other countries successful. We used to have always, even if we weren't doing well, we had the lowest interest rate in the world. Now they just keep raising the rate. But the fact is we're blowing through that and all the smoke and we are doing numbers that nobody's ever believed even possible.

articles.title_orig: Nvidia Stock Has A Cockroach Problem. What Comes Next Could Be Worse
articles.title_zh: Nvidia Stock Has A Cockroach Problem. What Comes Next Could Be Worse
articles.content_orig:
Nvidia’s leadership sought to set a path forward on Tuesday’s earnings call in the wake of former CEO Jensen Huang’s departure — defying calls to re-hire him, reassuring investors that demand for Nvidia’s products remains strong, and indicating that the leadership shakeup could prompt a new or more cautious approach to key elements of the company’s business.
The company has been rocked by scandal, national security concerns and the resignation of Huang, its founder and CEO of 33 years. And leadership was under pressure to reassure nervous investors Tuesday evening, with Nvidia having lost $751 billion in market value since last Sunday.
Many lingering questions remain. But investors appeared at least somewhat mollified by the comments and earnings results: shares ticked up nearly 5% in after-hours trading following the call.
Nvidia rules out Jensen Huang’s return as CEO, tells investors ‘we’ve got this’
Nvidia Board Chair Harvey Jones kicked off the earnings call by saying the board does not intend to reinstate Huang as CEO, despite Huang’s statement earlier Tuesday that he would be “honored” to return should the board allow it.
Jones said the board has “every confidence” in CFO and interim CEO Colette Kress to lead the company as it searches for a permanent replacement. He added the board wants to install a permanent CEO “as quickly as possible,” but it wouldn’t rush to appoint someone until it finds “exactly the right person.”
The board is considering internal and external candidates for the role. And while Jones offered no further hints on who is under consideration, Ian Buck, Nvidia’s vice president and general manager of Hyperscale and High-Performance Computing, joined Kress to take analyst questions on the call — a signal of his importance as a senior leader at the company.
Jones indicated that the board is taking the national security concerns into consideration in its search.
“The board appreciates that we’re living in a world where the advanced silicon technologies and national security dynamics are making major changes in our marketplace,” Jones said. “Our new CEO will have to navigate those waters very carefully.”
Why crisis at NVIDIA reverberates across the AI industry
Nvidia has played a key role in fueling the growth of the AI ecosystem by providing financing and investment to its customers to purchase its chips and build AI infrastructure.
Some industry analysts have questioned whether that will continue without Huang, who was considered the industry’s master dealmaker, even as others criticized the practice as “circular financing” that has artificially inflated the market.
Kress said on the call that the company has committed more than $100 billion to such deals as of the end of the quarter ended in October. However, she indicated that the company will carefully evaluate any deals to back would-be customers going forward.
“We remain thoughtful in how we participate and disciplined in how we commit capital,” Kress said. “We are proud of the role that we have played so far in supporting the ecosystem. As the market matures and additional sources of capital become available, we are rigorously evaluating future investments, commitments, and guarantees.”
Beyond its existing deals, Nvidia will take “a very strong look in terms of the types of companies that we would want to help in terms of the financing,” she said.
The company earned $2.4 billion in sales of licensed chips to China during the third quarter — comprising just over 2% of the total revenue in its core data center business unit. But the company has ceased shipments to the country, Kress said during Tuesday’s call.
That news comes as the company faces increased scrutiny from US officials over the potential illicit transfer of its chips to China.
How the Nvidia scandal lifted the curtain on a loophole that’s giving China access to US chips
A complex network of loopholes of shell corporations and unauthorized brokers, often operating via countries like Singapore, are believed to have enabled the transfer of millions of Nvidia chips to China in violation of export controls. Dan Ives, partner and senior managing director at Yorkville Ives & Co., estimated that China and Hong Kong “could comprise roughly 15%” of Nvidia’s previous revenues “when considering potential loopholes throughout Asia.”
The Commerce Department on Monday announced tighter export restrictions to prevent China from accessing sensitive, AI-powering computer chips via data centers in third-party countries.
The company is assuming no revenue from sales of licensed chips to China in the fourth quarter.
Even prior to Huang’s exit, questions were swirling about whether major tech companies might pull back on their spending on AI infrastructure as they face scrutiny from investors over when the technology will produce meaningful returns.
But Kress said demand for Nvidia’s products continues to outstrip supply, especially as a growing slate of companies and consumers seek to implement computing-intensive AI agents .
“Even in the last week, the continued ask is: How are we going to receive more and more supply to help (customers) with the demand that they have in front of them,” Kress said.
That growing demand pushed the company’s projection for full-year revenue growth in 2028 to 75%, up from its earlier projection of 70%. Nvidia also reported better-than-expected guidance for sales in the final quarter of this year.
“We’ve engaged with our customers, we’ve engaged with our suppliers, our partners,” following Huang’s resignation, Kress said. “They’re all 100% behind us.”

articles.title_orig: Oh No, I Can’t Stop Watching People Play ‘GTA VI’
articles.title_zh: Oh No, I Can’t Stop Watching People Play ‘GTA VI’
articles.content_orig:
12:31 PM EST on November 22, 2026
I did not imagine that the release of Grand Theft Auto VI would have any meaningful impact on my life, for the simple reason that I am not a gamer. I know and even respect a few people for whom video games are important, but I mainly regard this in the same way I do friends who really like square dancing, or go to church: nice for them, but not really my business.
And while I have, in the past, dated gamers and even come to occasionally enjoy watching them play video games, that was mainly because I'm bossy and liked telling them go over there or open that box I bet there's something inside. Backseat driving a video game can be fun but only insofar as I can manipulate what's happening. The appeal of Twitch, where you are simply one of dozens or hundreds of spectators watching someone else play a game has always been totally, utterly alien to me. This would be true even without the dangers of encountering slurs in a chat or being confronted by the ever present sight of anything that could be reasonably called "a gaming rig." No thank you.
And yet, I have found my conviction wavering recently as I find myself strangely compelled to click on clip after clip of people playing GTA VI . It started innocently enough, as people kept insisting that this game was teaching men to be thoughtful partners. I watched clips of people doing things Lucia will appreciate: buying groceries, taking her shopping, picking up flowers. I watched a guy make thoughtful decisions about how she might like to wear her hair. Soon I'd moved on to following along as people make Jason lovingly turn their house into a home , or invite Lucia to take the driver's seat on an aquatic adventure.
Before long, my attention ranged beyond the tender dynamics of this romance between down-on-their-luck criminals. I was enthralled by this one streamer pretending to host a nature documentary while wandering around the wilderness of Leonida (fake Florida.) I cheered as Jason is, for reasons that remain completely beyond me, rescued by a dog driving a jetski . I even found myself beguiled by the many ways a digitally rendered human body can react to getting hit by a basketball.
Finally, I felt something definitively crack open in my heart as I watched this man in raptures about the game's authentic depiction of a transmission tower:
Enjoy this guy getting bricked over the detail of towers in GTA6
I do not know what this means for me, and perhaps it will pass. I still have no intention of buying a console, or doing anything as unseemly as joining Twitch. But it would be dishonest to go on pretending that I am unmoved by this video game. Just look at those towers, boys. Just look at them.

articles.title_orig: Russia-bound ship towed away after it was attacked in Gulf of Finland
articles.title_zh: Russia-bound ship towed away after it was attacked in Gulf of Finland
articles.content_orig:
A Russian cargo vessel that was hit by a drone attack in the eastern Gulf of Finland is being towed away, authorities have said.
The Sparta II had been bound for Russia's Baltic exclave Kaliningrad when it was hit on Saturday morning, sparking a fire aboard.
It then drifted into Finnish waters and its crew were evacuated to Russia. Finnish defence forces said Ukraine was likely behind the attack. Kyiv has yet to comment.
Finland's Border Guard said on Sunday afternoon that fire was no longer visible from the outside but thermal cameras showed that some containers on the ship were still warm.
The Sparta II was "slightly listing", Finnish authorities added, but the "situation is stable" and no fuel or other "hazardous substance leaks" had been detected.
Kaliningrad Governor Alexei Besprozvannykh said two drones appeared to have been used in the strike and that there was "no threat" to his territory's supplies.
The Sparta II was sanctioned by the US in 2022 and Ukraine earlier this year, and is run by a Russian company, according to the Ukrainian and US governments.
The company says it was established within the structure of Russia's defence ministry in 2011 and since 2015 has been operating within the military construction complex.
Finland's coast guard said it had been alerted to the attack at around 08:50 local time (06:50 GMT) on Saturday and that the cargo vessel had been located approximately 50km west of the island of Suursaari in the Gulf of Finland.
This prompted "temporary aviation and maritime restrictions" around the area, Finnish border officials said.
"War is spilling over into our immediate vicinity," Finnish Prime Minister Petteri Orpo said. "Ukraine has the right to fight back against the aggressor."
Shortly after the incident, Finland's defence ministry said a Russian helicopter was suspected of violating the country's airspace, potentially linked to "rescue or tracking operations".
While Besprozvannykh initially said the crew of the Sparta II intended to repair the ship and carry on their journey, the Finnish Border Guard later said they had been evacuated to another Russian vessel that was en route to Russia.
Jukka-Pekka Lumilahti, director of maritime operations at the Finnish Border Guard, said during a news conference on Sunday that one Sparta II crew member had suffered minor injuries.
The Russian rescue vessel Murman is leading towing operations with the support of a Finnish guard ship and a Estonian naval patrol vessel.
Kaliningrad is a Russian exclave that sits between Poland and Lithuania.
Finnish Defence Minister Antti Häkkänen said that the Border Guard was responsible for the investigation into the attack and was co-operating with other relevant authorities.
Nato has also been informed, the defence ministry said.
The Baltic Sea has become a flashpoint in the Russia-Ukraine war, triggered when Russia launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. Ukraine has recently ramped up its long-range attacks against Russia beyond the front lines.
Earlier this month, a Ukrainian drone strike hit a Russian warship in the Gulf of Finland .

articles.title_orig: Court bans China’s BYD from selling ‘Defender clone’ SUV in EU
articles.title_zh: Court bans China’s BYD from selling ‘Defender clone’ SUV in EU
articles.content_orig:
Reactions to ICJ ruling underline global divisions over court with China raising concerns about judicial overreach
The US has greeted with caution the world’s highest court’s ruling that Myanmar committed genocide against its Rohingya minority, while China has raised concerns of judicial overreach.
Reactions to Thursday’s historic ruling underlined deep international division over the role of the court and similar institutions. The international court of justice (ICJ) had never previously found a state responsible for genocide and the decision could set a precedent for future genocide claims, notably a case against Israel .
The EU hailed a “landmark” judgment from the ICJ, while the UK reaffirmed “full support” for the court and the international legal order. Australia called on Myanmar to comply fully with the judgment and its obligations under international law.
But China, which has offered rare international support for Myanmar’s military rulers since they seized power five years ago, highlighted “issues such as jurisdiction overreach and expanded interpretation”.
“China … believes that such practices are not conducive to the settlement of disputes,” the foreign ministry spokesperson, Guo Jiakun, told a news briefing when asked about the ICJ ruling. “The international community should make joint efforts in this direction to avoid complicating this issue.”
Western nations cut ties with the unstable and poor south-east Asian country after the 2021 coup that ousted a civilian-led government.
Myanmar’s presidential spokesperson said on Friday that the ruling was “unfair”, noting the judges’ nine to six vote. The country’s military rulers have denied carrying out a genocide, claiming their actions targeted a Rohingya militant group that conducted insurgent attacks.
“When we look at the result, not all 15 judges agreed with the decision,” said Khaing Khaing Soe, speaking at a press conference in the capital, Naypyidaw. “So this was not a unanimous decision … I would say it is not fair.”
The US state department said on Thursday that Washington was examining the judgment, while stressing the need to avoid “politicisation” of the ICJ.
Donald Trump’s administration has taken a dim view of international law, vowing to dismantle the international criminal court (ICC), but has yet to question the legitimacy of the ICJ.
The state department reiterated US support for the people of Myanmar and said it shared “grave concerns over the continued abuses of human rights against Rohingya Muslims and members of other minority groups”, noting that the US was the largest single humanitarian donor to the Rohingya humanitarian crisis response.
In Brussels, the EU said Myanmar must fully implement the ICJ’s ruling “without delay” and that “compliance with ICJ’s decisions is not optional, it is an obligation under international law”.
“The European Union holds the ICJ in the highest regard and remains steadfast in its support for its critical role in the peaceful resolution of disputes and the upholding of the rule of law at international level,” an EU spokesperson said in a statement .
“The Rohingya people have endured immense suffering, including displacement and violence, and their plight must not be forgotten. This landmark ruling underscores the imperative of justice for victims and the necessity of upholding international law.”
The UN secretary general, António Guterres, called the ruling “a demonstration of international justice and a reaffirmation that impunity for such horrific acts must not stand”.
The UK expelled Myanmar’s defence attache and called for measures to “ensure the court’s ruling sends a clear message that such crimes cannot be committed with impunity”.
The ruling caps a lengthy legal campaign since August 2017 when Myanmar’s military launched what it called a “clearance campaign” in Rakhine state in response to an attack by a Rohingya insurgent group. Reports rapidly emerged of mass rapes and killings by security forces, as well as the burning of thousands of homes.
Judges rejected Myanmar’s claim that its actions were primarily intended as counter-terrorism operations, or even that they were an attempt to punish or forcibly displace the population but without committing genocide.
The country’s leader, Min Aung Hlaing, who headed the military during the 2016-17 attacks, has a pending arrest warrant from the ICC – which, unlike the ICJ, prosecutes individuals and not states – on allegations of crimes against humanity.
The former general overthrew the elected government of Aung San Suu Kyi, triggering a civil war that has left tens of thousands dead. He was installed as civilian president in April after elections that were widely discredited .
While the ICJ does not have the power to enforce rulings, its decisions are considered binding, carry diplomatic weight and can shape international action, including sanctions.
Under the 1948 convention, to establish that genocide occurred the court had to find that there was an intent to destroy the Rohingya “in whole or in part”.
About 1.2 million Rohingya refugees now live in Bangladesh, primarily in crowded camps across the Cox’s Bazar district, where they endure harsh conditions marked by fire hazards, infectious diseases, monsoon landslides, inadequate sanitation and strict work restrictions.
Judges at the court based in The Hague have also been asked to rule on other allegations of genocide.
South Africa has accused Israel of breaching the genocide convention during its offensive in Gaza, a claim Israel vehemently denies. That case is years from completion. An interim ICJ judgment in 2024 ordered Israel to ensure its forces do not commit acts of genocide against Palestinians in Gaza.
Ukraine also has a case pending against Russia . Shortly after Moscow’s full-scale invasion in February 2022, Kyiv accused Russia of fabricating genocide claims against Ukraine to justify the attack.

articles.title_orig: Russian attack near Ukraine’s capital strikes apartment building, killing 3 and burying others
articles.title_zh: Russian attack near Ukraine’s capital strikes apartment building, killing 3 and burying others
articles.content_orig:
Drone attacks blamed on Sudan’s paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF) have killed four people in and around the capital, Khartoum, and damaged a United Nations building, according to local reports and UN officials.
The attacks early on Sunday struck residential areas as Sudanese air defences responded to drones reportedly targeting government buildings and Khartoum’s airport.
The strikes have raised fresh concerns about the growing danger to civilians and aid workers as Sudan ‘s war increasingly relies on drones.
Explosions were heard across the capital between approximately 2am (00:00 GMT) and 4:30am (02:30 GMT), according to witnesses cited by the AFP news agency, as the army attempted to intercept the drones.
Al Jazeera’s AlMigdad Alruhaid reported from the city of Omdurman, across the Nile from Khartoum, that three people were killed and nine wounded when a drone struck a home in northern Omdurman.
A child was also killed in a separate attack south of the capital.
In the village of Jebel Aulia, about 45km (28 miles) south of Khartoum, a witness told AFP that a drone hit the home of a mosque official who calls worshippers to prayer. Residents searched the wreckage for trapped relatives.
The UN’s humanitarian coordinator in Sudan, Denise Brown, said on Sunday that one of its buildings had been damaged while staff were inside.
The UN’s humanitarian office, which coordinates emergency relief, condemned the danger to its personnel in a civilian neighbourhood, calling it “unacceptable”.
A Sudanese army source told AFP on Sunday that the drones had been launched from neighbouring Ethiopia’s Bahir Dar airport. The allegation could not be independently verified.
Ethiopia has previously denied Sudanese accusations that it allows the RSF to carry out attacks from its territory.
Sudan has also lodged complaints with the UN Security Council, the body responsible for international peace and security, and the African Union, a continental organisation, over alleged drone operations originating in Ethiopia.
Separately on Sunday, Sudan’s government accused RSF fighters of executing captured soldiers in southeastern Blue Nile state, near the Ethiopian border.
The government condemned the alleged killings as violations of international humanitarian law. The accusation has not been independently verified.
Both the RSF and the Sudanese army are relying more frequently on drones to hit enemy targets. More than 1,100 were killed by drones in the first half of this year, according to the United Nations.
The UN Children’s Fund (UNICEF) has said that drone attacks account for about two-thirds of children killed or injured in Sudan from the period of January to September.
The war in Sudan between the army and the RSF began in April 2023. It has led to one of the world’s worst humanitarian crises, with 13 million people displaced and some regions facing famine.

articles.title_orig: Delta tech issue delays hundreds of flights in and out of Atlanta ahead of Thanksgiving
articles.title_zh: Delta tech issue delays hundreds of flights in and out of Atlanta ahead of Thanksgiving
articles.content_orig:
NBC NEWS PROJECTION: Democrats secure the largest House majority for either party since 1992
A problem with the system Delta Air Lines uses to calculate aircraft weight and balance delayed its flights nationwide Sunday as Thanksgiving travel got underway.
The Federal Aviation Administration lifted its ground delay program for Atlanta-bound Delta flights at 11:26 a.m. ET, but by 1:55 p.m. ET, 997 flights into and out of Hartsfield-Jackson Atlanta International Airport had been delayed and 26 had been canceled, according to FlightAware.
The FAA briefly halted Atlanta-bound flights Sunday morning, then replaced the ground stop with a program that allowed flights to depart at staggered times. The delay program, requested by Delta, applied to the airline and its regional carriers flying into Hartsfield-Jackson from the contiguous United States.
The FAA had projected delays of 57 minutes on average and lasting up to 1 hour and 51 minutes.
Delta said it was working to restore the automated system that calculates how much a plane weighs and how that weight is distributed before takeoff. The airline said it was coordinating with air traffic controllers to prevent congestion at gates and on the tarmac in Atlanta.
Hartsfield-Jackson said the disruption was limited to Delta and did not affect airport operations broadly. The airport urged travelers to check their flight status with their airline and arrive at least two hours before domestic flights and three hours before international flights.
The delays at Hartsfield-Jackson came after the FAA issued a nationwide ground stop on Nov. 13 because of a technical issue with its air traffic control network. Flights resumed later that evening, but travel disruptions continued through the weekend.
A separate system outage delayed United Airlines departures on Nov. 16, disrupting crew communications and the airline’s ability to send pilots final aircraft weight data, according to the union representing United pilots. United said it resolved the issue that day.
Jay Blackman is an NBC News producer covering such areas as transportation, space, medical and consumer issues.

articles.title_orig: Climate change talks fall apart in final hours over fossil fuels
articles.title_zh: Climate change talks fall apart in final hours over fossil fuels
articles.content_orig:
COP31 President Murat Kurum, center, leaves a closing plenary session at the U.N. Climate Summit, Sunday, Nov. 22, 2026, in Antalya, Turkey. Nearly 200 countries failed to reach an agreement on whether they should move away from fossil fuels like coal and natural gas. Khalil Hamra/AP hide caption
ANTALYA, Turkey — International climate change talks in Antalya, Turkey, broke down in overtime hours over the main cause of planetary warming — fossil fuels. On Sunday, nearly 200 countries failed to reach an agreement on whether they should move away from energy sources like coal and natural gas.
The talks ended in a dramatic fashion, with the European Union negotiators saying they could not agree to a final agreement without mentioning the transition away from fossil fuels — the primary driver of climate change. The EU bloc then walked out of the room. Burning fossil fuels like oil, gas and coal make up roughly 73% of global emissions .
After representatives of the EU walked out, other countries also objected – including Panama and island states such as the Marshall Islands.
The European climate chief, Wopke Hoekstra, said that when the world is heading for an overshoot of 1.5 degrees, the EU could not tolerate an agreement that does not mention fossil fuels. "That is not acceptable," Hoekstra told reporters after walking out of the talks. "We do that with a heavy heart with many other countries, but we simply cannot accept this."
This is the first U.N. climate summit where there's been scientific consensus that the world will surpass a key global warming threshold. Countries agreed in 2015 to limit climate change to 1.5 degrees Celsius (2.7 degrees Fahrenheit), but the planet has essentially reached that limit already.
Negotiations at this year's U.N. Climate Summit were supposed to end Friday but there was no agreement on language about fossil fuels. Activists demonstrated by holding signs that read "shame" at COP31, Friday, Nov. 20, 2026, in Antalya, Turkey. Khalil Hamra/AP hide caption
Passing that threshold means more severe climate impacts , like more intense hurricanes and heat waves. The United Nations found that a best-case scenario of 1.7 or 1.8 degrees Celsius would require cutting emissions immediately, reducing them by 45% by 2035 . That, scientists say, would require dramatically cutting fossil fuel use.
"It's good that that decision has been rejected," says Mohamed Adow of Power Shift Africa, a nonprofit focused on climate change in Africa. "It doesn't have enough to help protect the people who are most vulnerable to climate change, who have contributed the least and are now suffering firsthand the worst."
NPR correspondent Michael Copley contributed to this story. This story was edited by Sadie Babits .
A previous version of this story incorrectly said the European Union walked out along with other countries. In fact, EU representatives walked out while other countries objected.

articles.title_orig: Coroner's concerns over delays after baby's death
articles.title_zh: Coroner's concerns over delays after baby's death
articles.content_orig:
A coroner has raised concerns about ambulance and medical delays after a 19-day-old baby boy died from sepsis and meningitis.
Sixteen days after Ezrah Pollard's birth in March 2022 he became unwell and was grizzly, not feeding and having a foul nappy.
A Truro inquest heard he developed a fever and a 111 call was transferred to the South Western Ambulance Service Trust (SWAST) which said he needed an ambulance response which should have arrived within 18 minutes.
An ambulance was chased over an hour later but it was not dispatched due to operational pressures - at the time of the incident they were taking four hours on average to respond to cases in the same category.
His parents took him to the Royal Cornwall Hospital in Truro where staff recognised that he was profoundly ill, the inquest heard.
He was transferred to Bristol Royal Hospital the next day where a CT scan revealed a devastating brain injury and he died on 25 March 2022.
Following the inquest, senior Cornwall coroner Andrew Cox wrote a Prevention of Future Deaths report.
He said he was concerned there was no pathway for an infant up to the age of three months to have a Category 1 ambulance disposition.
He said neither the 111 service or ambulance trust could give Ezrah's parents any guidance about the possible delay in an ambulance arrival.
Cox's report added parents should be advised to take a child to hospital immediately but it is understood the scripts followed by telephone dispatchers or non-medically qualified health advisors do not mandate this.
It said: "Ezrah required immediate antibiotics, yet their administration was avoidably delayed."
Ezrah's parents had to repeat details of his condition to the ambulance service and again in hospital because the staff there were not aware of that previous history, which potentially delayed treatment.
Responding to the coroner's report, SWAST said its emergency medical dispatchers (EMD) "do not have sufficient training or expertise to be able to identify a patient with Group B Streptococcus, nor definitely identify a patient with sepsis".
The Trust said they were "not expected to provide a diagnosis based on the symptoms described" and "given they are not clinicians, it would not be appropriate for an EMD to provide self-conveyance advice outside of the Standard Operating Procedure which is used during periods of escalation where we are experiencing capacity pressures due to high demand".
It said it takes the issue of ambulance delays very seriously and significant work has been done with partners to improve response times, but does not give people estimated tome of ambulance arrivals.
The Royal Cornwall Hospitals Trust said there are no extra systems available that would help more effective information sharing than those already in place.
All patients must undergo a formal triage assessment to confirm the patient's identity, current clinical condition and ensure that care is prioritised appropriately and is a key clinical safety measure, a spokesperson said.
Kernow Health CIC, which operates the 111 service in Cornwall said it was "unaware of a restriction in requesting a Category 1 ambulance" and it was "not currently usual practice to advise on waiting times for ambulance arrival".

articles.title_orig: Taiwan warns Canada over dependence on China
articles.title_zh: Taiwan warns Canada over dependence on China
articles.content_orig:
U.S.-China commission leaders warn of growing Chinese military capabilities, threats to Taiwan and risks to American security ahead of Trump’s summit with Xi and Putin.
President Donald Trump faces a potentially dangerous "two versus one" negotiating scenario when he meets with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin, two senior members of a congressional China watchdog warned Wednesday, raising concerns that Beijing could seek concessions on Taiwan while Moscow pushes for greater U.S. pressure on Ukraine.
"I think it is two versus one. We have China and China's junior partner, Russia," Randall Schriver, chairman of the U.S.-China Economic and Security Review Commission, told Fox News Digital in a Zoom interview. "Largely they come to the table as a team versus President Trump and the United States," he said, citing China's support for Russia's war in Ukraine.
TRUMP ARRIVES IN PHILIPPINES AHEAD OF XI JINPING SUMMIT IN CHINA AFTER GOP MIDTERM LOSSES
President Donald Trump greets Russian President Vladimir Putin as President Xi Jinping watches, before the welcome banquet at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit in Shenzhen, China, Nov. 18, 2026. (Iori Sagisawa/Pool via Reuters)
The warning comes ahead of Thursday's planned trilateral meeting in Shenzhen, China , on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit. The high-stakes talks are expected to address issues such as the wars in Ukraine and Iran, trade and nuclear weapons.
Mike Kuiken, the commission's vice chairman, echoed Schriver's assessment, arguing that Moscow's growing dependence on Beijing puts Trump at a disadvantage.
"Putin is a client state of Xi Jinping, and that essentially means that President Trump is in the room with a two against one scenario, and the stakes are significant," Kuiken told Fox News Digital.
"China is fueling Russia's war machine in Ukraine, and they are basically the lifeblood of the Russian economy at this point," he added.
TRUMP TO CONFRONT XI AT HIGH-STAKES SUMMIT OVER CHINA BACKING FOR IRAN, RUSSIA
Vladimir Putin shakes hands with Xi Jinping at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation Leaders' Summit in Shenzhen, China, Nov. 18, 2026. (Sputnik/Sergei Bobylyov/Pool via Reuters)
The commissioners spoke as the bipartisan body released its 2026 annual report to Congress , detailing Beijing's expanding military, technological and economic capabilities and the growing challenges they pose to American national security.
Asked what would constitute success or failure at the summit, Kuiken suggested Beijing would not have agreed to the meeting without assurances that its interests would be protected.
"My assessment is that the Chinese would never have agreed to this meeting if they had not had significant assurances that essentially nothing would happen," Kuiken said.
Schriver warned that both Xi and Putin would seek opportunities to advance their strategic objectives. He suggested Beijing would pursue gains related to Taiwan, while Moscow would hope Trump emerged from the meeting prepared to increase pressure on Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy .
CHINA'S XI SURPRISES TRUMP AT TARMAC, RECIPROCATING GESTURE SHOWN MONTHS AGO
President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping meet at the Great Hall of the People on May 14, 2026, in Beijing, China. (Alex Wong/Getty Images)
"If Putin had his way, Trump would emerge from the meeting and put more pressure on Zelenskyy," Schriver said.
He also questioned whether sufficient diplomatic groundwork had been laid for meaningful nuclear arms control discussions, one of the issues Trump has indicated he wants to address.
"President Trump would like to talk about nuclear disarmament, probably an agenda that makes sense. I'm just not sure we've done the front-end work when it comes to interagency work, bilateral or trilateral work, at a lower level to have a productive discussion there," Schriver said.
Nevertheless, Schriver suggested that avoiding concessions could itself represent a successful outcome for Washington.
"I think holding ground and just a restatement of U.S. interests is probably a victory of sorts for us," he said.
Responding to the commissioners' warnings, a spokesperson for the Chinese Embassy in Washington defended the trilateral meeting as an opportunity for cooperation among the three powers. "The three presidents will have an in-depth exchange of views on safeguarding world peace and enabling strategic stability in major-country relations. The summit is of groundbreaking significance," the spokesperson told Fox News Digital.
The spokesperson emphasized the three nations' shared responsibilities as permanent members of the U.N. Security Council, arguing that closer communication would serve global stability. "It is in the interest of the three countries to strengthen communication, manage differences and maintain stable relations. This is also the expectation of the international community and is conducive to global stability and dialogue and cooperation," the spokesperson said.
CHINA’S IRAN TIES COMPLICATE TRUMP-XI SUMMIT AS TENSIONS TEST US LEVERAGE
The Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company (TSMC) fabrication plant in Phoenix, Arizona, on March 3, 2025. (Rebecca Noble/Bloomberg via Getty Images)
Beyond the summit, the commissioners warned that the United States faces mounting challenges as China approaches 2027, the benchmark year associated with Xi's directive for the People's Liberation Army to develop the capability to conduct a Taiwan military operation.
Asked whether Washington was doing enough to deter Chinese military action against the self-governing island, Schriver gave a blunt assessment.
"I think the short answer is no, we're not doing enough," he said.
Schriver pointed to a pause in congressional notifications for U.S. arms sales to Taiwan , saying the commission wants those notifications to proceed and supports stronger security assistance for the island.
He also warned that Beijing's increasingly sophisticated coercion tactics extend beyond conventional military operations to include actions involving its coast guard.
"We do talk about counter coercion capabilities and blending not only military capabilities but law enforcement that the Chinese are doing, this sort of blended lawfare with their coast guard east of Taiwan," Schriver said.
Taiwanese conscripts during a visit by Taiwan's President Lai Ching-te to a military base in Taichung on June 28, 2024. (Sam YehAFP via Getty Images)
"It's a tough challenge as we're entering the benchmark year that Xi Jinping said of 2027. There should be more attention to this and there should be greater efforts to this."
Kuiken emphasized Taiwan's importance to the global technology supply chain, particularly its role in manufacturing advanced semiconductors used in artificial intelligence.
"Taiwan is the island at the center of the world. Xi Jinping is obsessed with it," he said.
Pointing to Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company, or TSMC, Kuiken warned of the broader implications for American technological leadership if Beijing were to take military action against the island.
He urged Washington and its partners to develop a coordinated strategy to make an invasion or other Chinese coercive measures against Taiwan unattractive to Beijing.
President Donald Trump meets with delegations from Japan, India and Australia at the Solaire Hotel, on Nov. 17, 2026, in Manila, Philippines. (Win McNamee/Getty Images)
Responding to concerns about Taiwan , a U.S. official told Fox News Digital, "There is no change to our policy with respect to Taiwan." Asked about the commissioners’ warnings, a White House official emphasized President Trump’s diplomatic approach to China and his plans to discuss nuclear arms reduction during the trilateral summit.
"Under President Trump’s leadership, U.S.-China relations have been refocused on what matters most – rebuilding the safety, security and prosperity of Americ

articles.title_orig: Yardeni Cuts S&P 500 Target Again, Says Bear Market Is Unlikely
articles.title_zh: Yardeni Cuts S&P 500 Target Again, Says Bear Market Is Unlikely
articles.content_orig:
The S&P 500 entered correction territory after U.S. stocks fell 3.7% Friday, leaving the index more than 10% below its recent peak after it broke its 200-day moving average. Ed Yardeni, president of Yardeni Research and one of Wall Street’s biggest bulls, said the selloff has gone too far and is a correction rather than a bear market, according to BeInCrypto.
Yardeni cited healthy corporate earnings and cheaper valuations, and still expects the S&P 500 to reach 8,500–9,000 by the end of 2027, though he sees no immediate trigger for a sharp recovery. Last year’s Liberation Day crash reversed after Trump changed course on tariffs, but investors may have to wait longer for a rebound this time. Federal Reserve Governor Christopher Waller said inflation remains a serious concern and raised the possibility of a half-point rate hike in December; markets expect further hikes in December and January. UBS strategist David Lefkowitz also expects slower growth and weaker AI spending. U.S. consumer sentiment rose roughly 7% in November to its highest level since August. Upcoming inflation data and December’s Fed decision will test whether rate hikes push the economy toward recession and undermine Yardeni’s recovery outlook.

articles.title_orig: Iranian attacks in the Strait of Hormuz are at the highest levels since the conflict began
articles.title_zh: Iranian attacks in the Strait of Hormuz are at the highest levels since the conflict began
articles.content_orig:
Reported attacks on shipping in and around the Strait of Hormuz are at the highest levels since the Iran war began, maritime data shows, as Tehran seeks to re-exert its control over the critical waterway amid falling oil prices.
In October, the number of attacks reported to the Royal Navy-affiliated United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations Centre (UKMTO) exceeded 30 for the first time since the US-Iran war began in late February.
As of Sunday, at least 22 attacks were reported in November, the second highest figure since the war began, according to a CNN analysis of UKMTO data. The reporting area covers the Strait of Hormuz, the Persian Gulf and the Gulf of Oman.
Before October, the number of reported attacks in the region averaged around 10 per month. Numbers vary, but data from the International Maritime Organization also points to October as having the highest number of confirmed incidents so far this year.
Since the conflict began, the strait has become a heavily contested frontier , with attacks there disrupting oil and gas shipping and sparking global economic fallout.
Iran began trying to halt traffic in the wake of the US-Israeli attacks that launched the war. In response, the US imposed a blockade on Iranian ports, and as CNN previously reported , Gulf producers have found ways of getting ships through the strait.
Commercial traffic through the channel – through which a fifth of the world’s oil passed before the war – remains at a reduced level when compared to the 2025 baseline.
As global oil prices fall and the Iran’s domestic crude revenues come under increasing strain, Tehran has been stepping up attacks, with experts saying the country is losing its leverage over the waterway and could escalate attacks further in an attempt to force concessions from Washington.
The International Energy Agency attributes the recent decline in oil prices to a recovery in Gulf exports. Prices also fell after the US midterm results as concerns over fresh US military action in the Middle East subsided.
“Markets appear to be increasingly assuming that a return to full-scale war is unlikely and that oil supplies will gradually recover,” Hamidreza Azizi, a senior Iran analyst at the International Crisis Group (ICG) think tank, told CNN . “But that assumption could change quickly if Iran decides to intensify the confrontation.”
Meanwhile, Iran’s domestic oil revenues are falling sharply as the US blockade of Iranian ports continues to stifle the country’s supply of oil to global markets, according to maritime data tracking service Kpler.
“Iranian oil on water outside the (US) blockade zone has hit zero as the last cargoes discharged in China earlier this month. Consequently, Iran’s oil revenues could drop to zero by mid-December,” Kpler reported in late October.
US President Donald Trump said this month the US doesn’t “need a deal” with Tehran and ordered Vice President JD Vance to turn his focus elsewhere .
“We don’t need a deal with Iran. Those days have long since passed!” Trump posted on Truth Social. “We’ve got their money, Hundreds of Billions of Dollars, and we’ve got their Strait!”
He later indicated he wouldn’t hesitate to resume military strikes in Iran if necessary.
During the latest attacks, projectiles struck three tankers exiting the strait on Friday and Saturday, according to Marisks, a maritime risk management company.
Marisks did not confirm who was behind the attacks, though it said Iranian involvement was “assessed as likely.”
Trump says Iran is ‘bullsh*tting’ on effort to end war
Fire erupted aboard the Captain Leon, a Marshall Islands-flagged chemical and oil tanker, after it was struck at the bow at 3 p.m. UTC (10 a.m. ET) on Friday. All crew were reported safe, Marisks said.
The Torkel, a Hong Kong-flagged crude oil tanker, caught fire after being hit in the stern at 5 a.m. UTC on Saturday (midnight ET on Saturday). Less than an hour later, the Arina, also Hong Kong-flagged, was struck in the engine room by a missile.
The attacks demonstrate the “continued critical threat” to commercial shipping in the region, Marisks said, particularly through the “southern corridor” near Oman’s coastline which Iran vehemently opposes.
CNN’s Eleni Giokos, Laura Sharman, Nadeen Ebrahim and Alayna Treene contributed reporting.

articles.title_orig: Drone attacks kill four near Sudan’s capital, damage UN building
articles.title_zh: Drone attacks kill four near Sudan’s capital, damage UN building
articles.content_orig:
Drone attacks blamed on Sudan’s paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF) have killed four people in and around the capital, Khartoum, and damaged a United Nations building, according to local reports and UN officials.
The attacks early on Sunday struck residential areas as Sudanese air defences responded to drones reportedly targeting government buildings and Khartoum’s airport.
The strikes have raised fresh concerns about the growing danger to civilians and aid workers as Sudan ‘s war increasingly relies on drones.
Explosions were heard across the capital between approximately 2am (00:00 GMT) and 4:30am (02:30 GMT), according to witnesses cited by the AFP news agency, as the army attempted to intercept the drones.
Al Jazeera’s AlMigdad Alruhaid reported from the city of Omdurman, across the Nile from Khartoum, that three people were killed and nine wounded when a drone struck a home in northern Omdurman.
A child was also killed in a separate attack south of the capital.
In the village of Jebel Aulia, about 45km (28 miles) south of Khartoum, a witness told AFP that a drone hit the home of a mosque official who calls worshippers to prayer. Residents searched the wreckage for trapped relatives.
The UN’s humanitarian coordinator in Sudan, Denise Brown, said on Sunday that one of its buildings had been damaged while staff were inside.
The UN’s humanitarian office, which coordinates emergency relief, condemned the danger to its personnel in a civilian neighbourhood, calling it “unacceptable”.
A Sudanese army source told AFP on Sunday that the drones had been launched from neighbouring Ethiopia’s Bahir Dar airport. The allegation could not be independently verified.
Ethiopia has previously denied Sudanese accusations that it allows the RSF to carry out attacks from its territory.
Sudan has also lodged complaints with the UN Security Council, the body responsible for international peace and security, and the African Union, a continental organisation, over alleged drone operations originating in Ethiopia.
Separately on Sunday, Sudan’s government accused RSF fighters of executing captured soldiers in southeastern Blue Nile state, near the Ethiopian border.
The government condemned the alleged killings as violations of international humanitarian law. The accusation has not been independently verified.
Both the RSF and the Sudanese army are relying more frequently on drones to hit enemy targets. More than 1,100 were killed by drones in the first half of this year, according to the United Nations.
The UN Children’s Fund (UNICEF) has said that drone attacks account for about two-thirds of children killed or injured in Sudan from the period of January to September.
The war in Sudan between the army and the RSF began in April 2023. It has led to one of the world’s worst humanitarian crises, with 13 million people displaced and some regions facing famine.
