articles.title_orig: Why have UN efforts to regulate ‘killer robots’ stalled?
articles.title_zh: Why have UN efforts to regulate ‘killer robots’ stalled?
articles.content_orig:
A United Nations conference has failed to agree on the swift adoption of legally binding rules to regulate autonomous weapon systems known as “killer robots”.
The member states of the Convention on Certain Conventional Weapons (CCW) met in Switzerland this week to discuss developing a new treaty which would regulate how the systems are used amid growing alarm over artificial intelligence (AI)-driven warfare and the lack of transparency and accountability.
But on Saturday, participants fell short of securing a mandate to negotiate a legally binding ban, agreeing instead to “elaborate” on a potential accord regulating such weapon systems by 2028. Rights groups and NGOs called the development “disappointing”.
Here’s what you should know:
According to the UN, lethal autonomous weapons systems are “a combination of one or more weapons and technological components operating together, that is capable of identifying, selecting, and engaging a target in a way that results in loss of life, without intervention by a human being operating the system”.
In simpler terms, they are systems that can identify, select and engage a target without human intervention. They are commonly referred to as “killer robots”, but this is not an established technical or legal designation.
The systems are programmed with a specific “target profile” before deployment, using sensor data such as facial recognition and other technologies to search for and kill matching targets.
“When the weapon encounters someone or something the algorithm perceives to match its target profile, it fires and kills,” the Autonomous Weapons Organisation explains.
According to the UN, not all autonomous weapon systems use AI. At the same time, AI is not necessary for autonomous weapon systems to function, nor does it determine whether a system is autonomous.
“However, when AI is used to identify, select and engage targets, it can amplify the serious legal, ethical, humanitarian and security concerns associated with autonomous weapon systems,” the UN warns.
Despite the concerns, AI-assisted weapons have already been used in the wars in Ukraine and Sudan and conflicts in the Middle East. Israel has used surveillance tools and AI-powered targeting systems in its genocidal war against Palestinians in the Gaza Strip.
Adopted in 1980, the CCW was established as a key international humanitarian law instrument.
“Its purpose is to ban or restrict the use of specific types of weapons that are considered to cause unnecessary or unjustifiable suffering to combatants or to affect civilians indiscriminately,” the UN says.
There is currently no legally binding instrument under the CCW that specifically regulates autonomous weapon systems.
The 128 countries that are party to the CCW met in the Swiss city of Geneva to discuss whether to authorise negotiations on curbs and a potential ban on such systems.
Julien Thoeni, the Swiss diplomat who chaired the Geneva conference, said the process should determine which weapons can be banned under international humanitarian law and which can be permitted but regulated.
The week-long conference came after nearly 100 countries agreed last month that it was important to swiftly adopt legally binding rules on the weapons capable of killing without a human making the final decision to fire.
But on Saturday, key arms-producing nations, including the United States, Russia and Israel, opposed the push. Decisions under the convention require the agreement of all member states.
Diplomats told the Reuters news agency that negotiations over the final wording of the treaty had continued all night after Russian objections to rules of procedure forced the cancellation of some formal meetings.
Two EU diplomats told media outlet Politico that the US, the UK, South Korea, Japan, Turkiye and Israel were also countries that resisted an effort to agree on a binding regulation. Others supporting a new convention included the European Union and NATO member states, as well as Ukraine, China and Iran, diplomats cited by The Guardian newspaper said.
In the end, all countries agreed on a watered-down convention which aims to develop new rules to regulate such weapons by 2028.
A diplomat involved in the talks from a country supporting the new laws told Reuters that the outcome was “disappointing but could have been much worse”.
While most countries support a pact to regulate “killer robots”, major military powers are opposing it, saying that humanitarian law linked to those weapons is sufficient.
As investment in AI warfare and autonomous systems grows, those countries also resist restrictions that could curb their ability to develop, test or use advanced weapons on modern battlefields. So rather than committing to strict legal obligations, they favour flexible, non-binding frameworks or longer timelines for discussions.
Swiss diplomat Thoeni told reporters after the meeting ended that some countries had rejected the word “negotiate”. The agreed text refers instead to the “elaboration” of an instrument.
Stop Killer Robots, a coalition of some 300 organisations opposed to the development and use of autonomous weapons, called the mandate “watered down” and said it offered no clear route to legally binding rules.
Its executive director, Nicole van Rooijen, said autonomous weapons were being deployed in combat, including systems that use artificial intelligence to choose targets.
“Delaying the creation of a legally binding instrument puts civilians and humanity at risk,” she told AFP news agency.
Critics also warned that without a binding treaty, the weapons objectify people and undermine their dignity by reducing human lives to sensor data and algorithmic targets.
Georgia Hinds, legal adviser at the International Committee of the Red Cross, said that “there is a fundamental ethical concern with having what are essentially these life-and-death decisions determined by programming, determined by an algorithm”.
“That’s not something that you can fix with better technology. That is a moral red line that we cannot cross,” Hinds added.

articles.title_orig: What’s behind Iran’s escalation of attacks in the Gulf?
articles.title_zh: What’s behind Iran’s escalation of attacks in the Gulf?
articles.content_orig:
The Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) claimed to have targeted radars at a United States military base in Bahrain, as Iran has intensified attacks over the past week, hitting tankers in the Strait of Hormuz, a global oil chokepoint, and downing US drones.
At least 25 tankers have been hit in and around the Strait of Hormuz, through which a fifth of global oil and gas passes, in the past seven days, causing the Gulf oil flow to drop sharply.
The escalating attacks come as Iran’s President Masoud Pezeshkian said his country is facing what he called a “silent economic war” amid US sanctions and a naval blockade.
So what is behind Iran’s latest escalation, and will it trigger a new round of hostilities between Tehran and Washington or force the two sides to sit down for talks to end the war that has caused a global energy crisis?
Bahrain has faced the brunt of Iran’s attacks in recent days.
On Saturday, Manama said an Iranian strike hit a civilian industrial facility, starting a fire , as it thwarted several other attacks that day.
The IRGC said it had carried out a combined missile and drone operation targeting US military positions at the al-Riffa and Awali bases in Bahrain, claiming to have destroyed two US Patriot air defence radars at the bases.
Iranian state media reported that an interceptor missile launched from the US Fifth Fleet base in Bahrain crashed on Sitra Island near Manama, sparking a large fire.
The IRGC said the operation was retaliation for a US strike on a radar installation on Iran’s Hengam Island. Iran has justified the attacks as a response to continued violations of its airspace, including by US MQ-1 and MQ-9 reconnaissance and combat drones.
Bahrain has faced three drone attacks in recent days after a lull in fighting for several weeks.
Iran’s army on Saturday said its air defences fired a missile at a US F-16 jet over the Gulf the previous evening, damaging the aircraft, the IRNA news agency reported. However, US Central Command (CENTCOM) denied the claim, stating that “all US fighter jets in the Middle East are safe and accounted for”.
Iranian forces on Sunday also said they shot down another MQ-1 drone east of the Strait of Hormuz. The IRGC claimed it was the 20th US drone of this type to be shot down since the war began in late February and the fourth in the past 24 hours.
Meanwhile, British maritime authorities reported two incidents involving tankers struck by unidentified projectiles in the Strait of Hormuz near Oman.
Al Jazeera correspondent in Tehran, Resul Serdar, said incidents involving tankers had increased sharply over the past week, with about 25 since November 14.
Last week, the Iranian army also said it targeted US drone and missile installations at Kuwait’s Ali Al Salem base. The attack came after the US struck Qeshm Island in the Strait of Hormuz, which remains under effective Iranian control.
Oil passing through the Strait of Hormuz has seen a considerable dip as Iran has escalated attacks on a near-daily basis.
According to the UK Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO), 263 ships passed through the key waterway between November 12 and 18, which is 15 percent fewer than the previous week and 20 percent fewer than the week before that.
Of those vessels, 37 were oil tankers, down from 52 the previous week, UKMTO reported on Friday.
The figures, however, could be higher as vessels passing through as part of shadow fleets are not officially registered.
About 135 ships passed daily through the vital strait before the war began in February.
Last week, the US maritime agency warned that the Iran blockade was adding to rising Gulf premiums, with insurance rates up from 0.10-0.25 percent before the war to 3.5-7.5 percent.
Oil prices have spiked, crossing $100 a barrel before settling down to $83, still more than $15 from before the war.
Cumulative losses from the conflict have now reached 2.8 billion barrels of oil and 60 billion cubic metres of gas supply from the Gulf, the International Energy Agency (IEA) said on Thursday.
The IEA, however, added that the conflict could cut world oil demand by more than 4 percent by 2035 if governments accelerate electrification, efficiency and fuel-switching measures in response.
As Iran has ramped up attacks, senior officials have asked the US to choose between surrendering to missiles or to diplomacy.
The attacks indicate that Iran is using its leverage in the conflict, sending the message that the US allies in the region will continue to bear the brunt of its actions if the war does not end.
The attacks aim to diminish US military capabilities in the region and “also to spread the pain of the war widely to include the entire [Gulf region] and, indirectly, global economies via higher shipping costs and stressed supplies of essentials”, Rami Khouri, a public policy fellow at the American University of Beirut, told Al Jazeera.
The single biggest driver of this strategy, Khouri said, is for Iran to continually ensure that it will no longer “suffer alone from US-Israel-imperial assaults”.
Tehran is hoping to change US policy by revealing its inability to protect its own facilities or those of its Arab allies, which could prompt Arab governments to press US President Donald Trump to end the war, Khouri, who is also a nonresident senior fellow at the Arab Center Washington DC, added.
Meanwhile, Deputy Foreign Minister Kazem Gharibabadi told Iranian media that he considers the economic blockade imposed by the US on Iran an act of war.
“We consider the economic siege a hostile act, and we will take any necessary measures to break this economic siege,” Gharibabadi told Iranian reporters.
The ongoing US naval blockade on Iran, overland trade disruptions and a wave of new sanctions imposed in August as part of Operation Economic Outcast are hurting Iran economically.
US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, who has led Washington’s sanctions regime against Tehran, has claimed the economic embargo will result in a 25 percent contraction of the Iranian economy by the year ending March 2027.
However, Iranian authorities insist they can withstand the economic pressure.
The strikes on US interests in the Gulf in recent days have therefore been viewed as a defiant response to the US campaign. But there are signs that the country’s economy and common Iranians are suffering from the current conditions.
Trump may choose to declare victory and walk away from the war on Iran rather than negotiate a deal, but continuing the naval blockade on Iran would risk further military escalation, says Trita Parsi, executive vice president of the Quincy Institute for Responsible Statecraft.
Speaking to Al Jazeera, Parsi said Trump was unlikely to accept an agreement that could be seen in Washington as showing the war had failed.
“If he continues the blockade, there will be escalation,” Parsi warned, arguing that Iran would not refrain from retaliating against continued economic pressure.
He said Trump would need to “slowly, perhaps imperceptibly, lift the blockade, as well as lift some of the sanctions” if he wanted to withdraw from the confrontation without renewed fighting.
Hassan Ahmadian, professor at the University of Tehran, said Iran is forcing a “binary” choice on Trump.
If Washington lets the tankers pass, the US blockade “ends without an agreement or war”, Ahmadian said on X. However, if the US attacks the vessels, it could face “Iranian responses that will be difficult for [Trump] to avoid”.
Trump said on Saturday he had plans to make a deal with Iran that is “permanent” and prevents it from getting a nuclear weapon.
He also told US broadcaster Fox News that he was never very interested in regime change in Iran, but called its new leadership “more rational”.

articles.title_orig: U.S. Stocks Extend Plunge as AI Boom Turns to Bust
articles.title_zh: U.S. Stocks Extend Plunge as AI Boom Turns to Bust
articles.content_orig:
A punishing sell-off in technology stocks intensified Friday, wiping out the Nasdaq Composite’s gains for the year, as investors continued to pull money out of the once high-flying AI trade.
The S&P 500 fell 3.7% and posted its seventh consecutive day of losses — its longest losing streak since February 2020, when Wall Street started bracing for what became the Covid pandemic.
The tech-focused Nasdaq faced even steeper losses on Friday, dropping 5.28%. It is now down more than 2% for the year.
The Nasdaq hit a record high on October 6, and was up as much as 18.7% on the year. Since that all-time high, the index has slumped, erasing all those gains and shedding roughly $8.7 trillion in market value.
“It’s a meltdown right now,” Arun Sundaram, senior vice president of investment strategy at CFRA Research, told CNN in an email. “So much bearish sentiment around tech and AI.”
Even Anthropic’s blockbuster stock market debut quickly lost its shine Friday, with shares in the AI lab dropping 8.5%. They closed at $88.91, just above the company’s IPO of $83.
Why Anthropic’s blockbuster debut didn’t ease Wall Street’s AI fears
The Dow fell 950 points, or 1.93%, posting its fifth consecutive day of losses of more than 1%. The Dow dropped 8% this week, its worst week since March 2020.
The Dow and the S&P 500 closed in correction on Friday, trading down more than 10% from their respective peaks on August 5 and October 6. They join the Nasdaq, which closed in correction earlier this month and is now down 18% since its record high on October 6.
Meanwhile, the Nasdaq and S&P 500 suffered their worst week since early April 2025, when President Donald Trump’s tariff plans rocked global markets.
Stocks associated with the AI trade have been in a serious rough patch for weeks now. But with Anthropic’s buzzy IPO now in the rear-view mirror, traders’ concerns about the broader industry are once again coming to the fore.
It’s the year of the mega AI IPO. Should you invest?
“There is a real exodus out of tech stocks,” Steve Sosnick, chief strategist at the online brokerage platform Interactive Brokers, told CNN. “Buy the dip has been taking a back seat to sell the rally – or just sell.”
“The tech sector is just getting walloped,” Sosnick said.
Investors are grappling with a bevy of concerns, from uncertainty over how newly elected Democratic governors will impact the pace of the data center buildout to uncertainty about the future of Nvidia’s role in powering the AI industry’s growth after CEO Jensen Huang resigned.
“There is a fear that maybe there is too much froth and enthusiasm in the tech bet given all the risks out there,” said David Kelly, chief global strategist at JPMorgan Asset Management.
Kelly noted that corrections are “inevitable” and there is “nothing particularly ominous” about a correction given how much US stocks have rallied in recent years.
“This is not a fatal illness. It’s not even the flu. At the moment, it looks like a mild cold, and it should be over in a week or two,” he said.
Another growing concern for investors: Companies are spending hundreds of billions of dollars on the AI buildout, using their own cash and also tapping the debt and equity markets to raise more capital.
For awhile, investors cheered the AI spending. But now, they’re getting more serious about demanding evidence of return on investment.
“The market was already questioning some of the cost-benefit analysis … and you’re coming off of relatively euphoric levels. Put all that together, that’s a lot for the market to bear,” Sosnick at Interactive Brokers told CNN.
In a sign of growing nervousness among investors, the VIX, which tracks expectations for volatility and is known as Wall Street’s ‘fear gauge,’ surged 86% this week and closed at 35.89 on Friday — its highest level in 19 months. Generally, a level above 20 indicates heightened investor uncertainty.
The sell-off sent investors looking for safer corners of the market, like US Treasury bonds, which rallied sharply on Friday.
Corners of the AI trade that have been in the spotlight in recent weeks were among the names under pressure. CoreWeave, the neocloud backed by Nvidia, slumped 12% Friday. CoreWeave’s IPO price in March 2025 was $40 a share — it’s trading at $39.51 now, wiping out all gains since it debuted on the market.
Trump defends Putin relationship and says he’ll stop US companies from building data centers abroad
Nvidia dropped 14% on Friday, its worst day in almost two years. The chip giant tumbled 22.9% on the week, posting its worst week since October 2008.
Reuters reported Friday that the US Securities and Exchange Commission is probing Nvidia over its accounting practices, adding to pressure on the stock.
Nvidia has plunged 47.5% since its October 6 peak, shedding $2.7 trillion in market value. That’s larger than the individual market value of every company in the S&P 500 except Apple, Microsoft, Alphabet and Nvidia itself.
The sell-off has been so severe that tech stocks may suddenly look cheap to some investors. US tech stock valuations, as measured by the forward price-to-earnings ratio of the S&P 500’s info tech sector, entered Friday at their lowest level since March 2020, according to FactSet.
As for Nvidia? The forward P/E ratio for the next 12 months is the lowest since 2002.
That has some strategists suggesting that widespread fears might be overblown.
“I don’t fully understand it, as the fundamentals don’t really justify all this selling,” said Sundaram from CFRA Research. “But right now, it’s sell now and worry about the fundamentals later.”

articles.title_orig: One Type of Exercise Could Be an Overlooked Treatment For Knee Osteoarthritis, Clinical Trial Finds
articles.title_zh: One Type of Exercise Could Be an Overlooked Treatment For Knee Osteoarthritis, Clinical Trial Finds
articles.content_orig:
Pain, swelling, and stiffness in the knees can be downright debilitating.
As cartilage breaks down in these joints, it can significantly reduce freedom of movement and cause pain, even when standing still or sitting.
Surprisingly enough, core exercises may be a neglected form of treatment for knee osteoarthritis.
A randomized controlled trial in India has now found that working out the abdominal muscles may have a trickle-down effect for the knees.
Strengthening the abdomen won't stop cartilage from degenerating, but in this particular trial, when core exercises were added to typical rehabilitation programs, it improved physical function more than conventional exercises alone.
What's more, patients who did the core exercises also reported significantly less pain when moving about.
The findings are published in Scientific Reports , and while the study is small, the methodology was rigorously designed.
The trial involved 100 participants, aged 40 to 80, with mild to moderate knee osteoarthritis.
Roughly half the group were randomized to partake in conventional knee-focused rehabilitation for 12 weeks.
During the trial, this half of the group partook in 45 minutes of supervised exercise three times a week for four weeks.
Each session involved progressive strengthening, range-of-motion, and functional exercises, such as straight-leg raises and moves to strengthen the quadriceps.
Participants then continued these exercises at home on their own for an additional 8 weeks.
Meanwhile, the other half of the group was randomized to undertake a different rehabilitation program.
This one involved a mix of conventional knee-based rehabilitation exercises and progressive core-targeting exercises.
The core exercises included abdominal bracing, glute bridges, forearm planks, arm raises while lying down, heel taps, and alternating arm-and-leg movements similar to dead bugs.
After the 12-week intervention period, both groups demonstrated significant reductions in resting pain.
But it was the group that also partook in core training that demonstrated greater improvements in physical function tests and reported less pain when moving about.
Importantly, this group also reported greater improvements in their quality of life.
The authors of the study don't know why core training led to these benefits, but they suggest that an improvement in posture control may help stabilize the body's core during exercise, putting less strain on the lower limbs.
"Collectively," the team concludes , "these biomechanical adaptations provide a plausible explanation for the greater improvement observed in pain, physical function, and quality of life compared with conventional knee-focused strengthening alone."
The findings are supported by previous research, which also suggests that the core is a neglected part of knee pain.
In 2021, for instance, a peer-reviewed narrative review argued that despite preliminary findings that core training is beneficial for knee issues, more research is needed.
"Investigations that show it is safe and effective in older adults have not been adapted to/incorporated into treatment recommendations for those with knee osteoarthritis," the authors argued.
This year, the results of several randomized clinical trials have begun to roll in.
One trial among 48 patients with knee osteoarthritis in Pakistan, for example, also found that adding core stability training to knee exercises produced greater improvements in pain, knee mobility, and quality of life after 12 weeks.
Plus, a larger study of 100 patients found that adding core exercises to conventional knee rehabilitation was more effective than adding foot-and-ankle strengthening.
That seemed to be particularly true for outcomes like pain and physical function.
Related: Study of 33,500 CT Scans Challenges a Common Assumption About Ab Strength And Back Pain
These randomized trials are small, but their findings suggest that exclusively targeting the joints during osteoarthritis treatment may not be the best move.
The whole body is connected, and the function of our extremities is founded upon the stability of our trunk.
Ab exercises may help cut to the core of the issue.
The research has been published in Scientific Reports .
This article was fact-checked by Rebecca Dyer and edited by Rebecca Dyer . While we pride ourselves on our process, we are only human. If you spot a mistake, please let us know .

articles.title_orig: What to know about US-China competition as Trump and Xi meet again this week - Periódico Digital Centroamericano y del Caribe
articles.title_zh: What to know about US-China competition as Trump and Xi meet again this week - Periódico Digital Centroamericano y del Caribe
articles.source: Periódico Digital Centroamericano y del Caribe
articles.content_orig:
This is read by an automated voice. Please report any issues or inconsistencies here .
See more from the L.A. Times in Google Search. Set us as preferred
SHENZHEN, China — Donald Trump met Thursday with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin at a villa in southern China, an unprecedented gathering of a U.S. president with Washington’s chief geopolitical rivals bent on undermining American power.
The meeting, conceived not by policymakers but by Trump and Putin, had a fractured agenda, with each leader coming to the table with divergent interests and different stakes.
As they dispersed to their capitals, the presidents had few tangible gains to show for a summit hastily assembled in a matter of weeks, bypassing the months of groundwork that typically underpin diplomatic breakthroughs.
But the image of Trump standing alongside Putin and Xi — then sitting alone with the two of them, at a great round table in a cacophonous hall — was itself the culmination of a decade of his foreign policy thinking, a great-man theory of diplomacy that has broken with American tradition, elevating authoritarian leaders over democratic allies.
The U.S. president appeared subdued, thanking Xi and Putin before turning to journalists.
“No peace was ever forged by declining opportunities for engagement and speech,” he said, arguing he had a “special responsibility” to maintain dialogue with adversarial world powers. “We are really making history.”
Unlike at Yalta in 1945, when President Franklin D. Roosevelt, British Prime Minister Winston Churchill and Soviet Premier Josef Stalin famously gathered to shape the postwar order, the American leader was not at the center of these photographs. That place of honor belonged to Xi, the host, who presided over the gathering at a remote retreat outside the city.
It was a portrait of a nation asserting its place among the world’s superpowers — the very image Beijing had sought in agreeing to host the extraordinary gathering.
“History tells us that when great powers are at peace, the world is secure,” Xi said. “When great powers clash, the world is in chaos.”
The competing agendas could make the summit little more than a spectacle, yet still produce images that harken back to the famous Yalta conference of 1945.
But if any substantive understandings were reached behind closed doors, none of them were released to the public.
The summit’s pageantry fit a familiar pattern for Trump, who has repeatedly staged headline-grabbing encounters with controversial leaders only to walk away empty-handed. Three high-stakes meetings with North Korean leader Kim Jong Un during his first term failed to meaningfully shift relations between Washington and Pyongyang, and a meeting with Putin in Anchorage last year likewise failed to generate progress toward ending Russia’s war in Ukraine.
This time, the spectacular gathering lasted just an hour and a half, and produced only a readout of four points of agreement, broadly committing to work to uphold international security, minimize nuclear risks, increase petroleum output and, most specifically, overhaul the United Nations and the International Criminal Court, which it said “must not abuse their jurisdiction.”
The court has a warrant outstanding for Putin’s arrest.
Putin framed the trilateral meeting as one of equals, elevating a Russian Federation that has been economically and militarily devastated, and ostracized from the international community, over its war against Ukraine. Russian state media highlighted Xi’s decision to place Putin to his right throughout the summit as a gesture of honor.
“I am convinced that Russia, China and the United States, our peoples, are capable of making a significant contribution to strengthening security and stability in the world,” Putin said, “if they cooperate constructively as partners on the basis of mutual respect, equality and a balance of interests.”
The Russian leader appeared almost giddy throughout the day’s meetings, and upon departing Shenzhen for the airport, escorted personally by Xi to his car, was heard saying, “I don’t think anyone ever expected everything to go so well.”
“The trilateral summit was a giant gift to Putin. It put him on a stage where he does not belong,” Michael McFaul, a former U.S. ambassador to Russia now at the Hoover Institution at Stanford, told The Times. “The photo of that meeting will be seen throughout the world, making it look like Putin is a respected leader of a great power. What did Americans get in return? Nothing, absolutely nothing.”
The unusual summit comes just weeks after Trump suffered a generational rebuke in the midterm elections and as he remains bogged down in a war with Iran, which threatened to erupt in a new round of hostilities in the coming days.
Publicly, Trump framed the gathering as an effort to curb nuclear proliferation. Yet instead of advancing a trilateral nonproliferation agreement among the world’s three largest nuclear powers, Putin offered a message of defiance, sending nuclear-capable bombers to nearby Vietnam a day before the summit in a rare deployment. China, meanwhile, rebuffed calls to slow down its breakneck nuclear buildup currently dwarfed by America’s arsenal.
The Trump administration let the last remaining U.S. arms control agreement with Russia expire earlier this year.
“Despite the talk of denuclearization by the Trump administration, no staff members prepped the president to meaningfully discuss this topic with Putin or Xi, who are unwilling partners for restraints and guardrails,” said Jennifer Hong, senior director of the Institute for Indo-Pacific Security.
Instead, Trump’s focus seems to have turned to ensuring nonproliferation not among world powers, but in the Middle East — the main justification he has given for launching war against the Islamic Republic this year.
“We’re not going to let Iran have a nuclear weapon,” he said at the start of the meeting.
Putin had hoped the summit would secure space and time to continue executing his war against Ukraine — a prospect that Ukraine’s president, Volodymyr Zelensky, took seriously as the meeting was about to begin.
“Big countries always think that they can make decisions about the future of all the world,” Zelensky told NBC News. “It’s a huge mistake.”
Sitting alongside Xi, Trump said the two of them were looking to “help with respect to the war with Russia and Ukraine” and “would like to see it ended.”
Few independent analysts believe Putin is interested in ending the war in its current state. But at the trilateral engagement, Trump suggested Zelensky was responsible for Moscow’s continued attempts at conquest. “Things are happening,” Trump said. “I think that [Putin] and I hope the other side, would like to see an end to that war.”
The meetings were Trump’s first with Putin since their summit last year in Alaska, a gathering that failed to produce a breakthrough in the Republican president’s attempts to bring an end to the deadliest conflict in Europe since World War II.
Trump met individually with  Putin and Xi ahead of the trilateral gathering despite White House officials insisting before the trip that a direct meeting with Putin was not on the agenda.
“Who is he? He’s my friend,” Trump said, walking toward Putin with an outstretched hand.
“We have had a great relationship for many years. We’ve known each other for a long time,” Trump added. “And I think a lot of wonderful things can come out of this, or at least start.”
A Russian diplomat attending the conference with Putin told reporters that Trump and Putin together are “committed to a peaceful resolution to the Ukrainian conflict, though the Europeans are clearly trying to stand in the way.”
European officials have been wary of the Shenzhen summit, warning against the future of Ukraine being negotiated without Ukrainians present. A Chinese official told The Times they would have been welcome to attend, but no invitation was formally extended.

articles.title_zh: Developers have released the Leonida tool for natively running Grand Theft Auto VI on PC.
articles.content_orig:
Leonida, an open source project aimed at statically recompiling the console version of Grand Theft Auto VI for Xbox Series X into a native OS application, has appeared on the GitHub platform. WindowsSince the console processor uses the x86-64 architecture, the authors of the initiative translate the console system calls into the PC environment, and translate the compiled RDNA2 graphics programs into the SPIR-V format for operation via the API. VulkanThe project is distributed under the GPL-3.0 license and does not contain any copyrighted game files, encryption keys, or executable modules. To build the port, the user will need an unpacked copy of version 1.0.2.1 of the game, from which the utilities will automatically extract the necessary assets and generate shaders locally on the computer.
At this stage the game does not launch yet, as the developers lack an executable file to complete the work on the loader and the D3D12 graphics layer for VulkanHowever, the toolkit already successfully extracts and converts all 26 game shaders to SPIR-V, as well as exports 503D models to OBJ format, textures to DDS, and audio tracks to Ogg Opus or WAV. Building the project independently on a PC requires certain software and hardware requirements.
The automated build script automatically finds the game folder on local drives using the MicrosoftGame.Config configuration, checks for the presence of the required components, and saves the finished result in the user's documents directory. WindowsThe process of resource extraction and shader validation is supported on Linux, where the executable loader can be launched via Wine or Proton. The project's repository already has over 8,2 stars and 147 contributors, who continue to refine the translation of graphics commands and the emulation of 64-thread shader groups for NVIDIA and Intel graphics cards.

articles.title_orig: South Korea’s Education Minister Resigns Over Anti-A.I. Cheating Rules
articles.title_zh: South Korea’s Education Minister Resigns Over Anti-A.I. Cheating Rules
articles.content_orig:
South Korea's Education Minister Choi Kyo-jin has resigned over an exam cheating scandal that shocked the nation.
He said he took full responsibility for the confusion caused by last-minute measures aimed at stopping AI-assisted cheating during Thursday's annual college entrance exam, known as Suneung.
A week ago, the top scorer in the national tax accountancy exam admitted using a mini-camera, mobile phone and AI tools. This prompted officials to act urgently to detect hidden devices, including sending emergency alerts to every single mobile phone in the country.
The Suneung takes up to nine hours to complete, and it plays a big role in career trajectories of millions of South Koreans.
"As the minister in charge, I believe I cannot escape criticism that we failed to prepare in advance," Choi was quoted as saying on Sunday by South Korea's Yonhap's news agency.
"Now that the exam has concluded, I feel a deep sense of responsibility and am offering my resignation," the minister added.
South Korean President Lee Jae Myung - who has been calling for an overhaul of the current exam system - later accepted Choi's resignation.
The education ministry earlier said 111 candidates had been found with unauthorised smart devices during this year's Suneung, which was taken by about 500,000 students.
Concerns over academic dishonesty during the fiercely competitive exam had been brewing in recent weeks, after reports of candidates cheating with the help of AI devices.
These fears came to a boil last weekend, when Han Won-seok, the top tax accountancy exam scorer in April, admitted to cheating.
His confession came amid speculation over his unusually high score, with just one out of 160 questions wrong.
"I used a microcamera to photograph the test questions and sent them to an AI, then checked my answers on my smartphone to commit the cheating," the 34-year-old said in a video message.
This prompted the authorities to introduce urgent measures, with just days ahead of the Suneung.
This included sending nationwide emergency alerts on the exam day.
Three alerts were sent between 08:00 and 15:00 local time on Thursday, causing phones across the country to blare out in unison - even if they were on silent mode, and even if they belonged to tourists using data roaming.
The phones did not ring out if they were switched off or on airplane mode.
It was the first time that South Korea used its national disaster alert system to catch exam cheaters.
Candidates also had to cover up the buttons on their shirts and jackets to block any hidden cameras, and authorities conducted inspections of eyewear.
All this made even honest test takers paranoid.
Ahead of the Suneung, one high school senior told the Korea Times he was worried his horn-rimmed spectacles would be mistaken for smart glasses.
Another told Yonhap he usually wore glasses but made an effort to put on contact lenses for the Suneung to avoid raising suspicions.

articles.content_orig:
By clicking â SIGN UP â you agree to our Terms of Use and Privacy Policy .
Vladimir Putinâs crusade to win over war veterans has been brutally exposed as a farce by members of his own party.
Since its inception in early 2024, the Russian leaderâs âTime of Heroesâ program has romanticized the Kremlinâs war against Ukraine and the meat-grinder tactics used by the military to keep feeding the war machine. It has signaled to both military veterans and the wider Russian public that those who have served on the battlefield will serve as the countryâs new âeliteâ and hold prestigious places in government.
That notion went up in flames this week after two local lawmakers from Putinâs United Russia party were caught using their supposed enthusiasm for the program to lure vulnerable men into a deranged scheme. After forcing the men to sign contracts to join the war, they arranged quick marriages before deployment and set up bank accounts to receive âdeath benefitsâ for their newlywed husbandsâ inevitable battlefield demise.
Irina Bezman showed off her new husband in a social media post nodding to the âtime of heroes.â
Federal investigators in Krasnoyarsk Krai detailed the bizarre plot in a press release announcing the chargesâthough they neglected to mention that two of the suspects were the face of Putinâs local âTime of Heroesâ program as deputies of United Russia.
The group first stole a one-time payment issued to one of the men for his military service in the amount of 1.8 million rubles ($22,000), and âfollowing the death of the service member, the group stole another 5 million rubles from his bank account,â investigators said.
They reportedly failed to get access to the bank account of the other duped groom.
The two women, identified in local reports as 41-year-old Irina Bezman and 64-year-old Galina Kalimulina, worked as deputies of the Sharypovo District Council and routinely posted about their support for the war.
It was one of their social media posts that reportedly triggered local scrutiny: Bezman, in a now-deleted post, shared a photo of herself with her new husband, Vladimir, holding up their marriage certificate at the local registration office.
Russian President Vladimir Putin (C), Prime Minister Dmitry Medvedev (L) and Defense Minister Sergei Shoigu (R) attend a wreath-laying ceremony at the tomb of the unknown soldier, on Feb. 23, 2015, in Moscow, Russia.
Sasha Mordovets/Getty Images
The local outlet Zapad24 reports that residents were immediately baffled to see the local councilwoman had married a man from a very different walk of life, known mainly for hanging out on a local churchâs steps and sweeping the courtyard.
Kalimulina, who had served as the executive secretary of the regional branch of United Russia, was described as the mastermind of the scheme.
She filled her social media pages with posts in support of the war and Russian troops, often signing off on them with the hashtag, âWe donât abandon our own.â

articles.title_orig: GTA 6 Is Blowing Away Gaming's Greatest Devs, Including Naughty Dog
articles.title_zh: GTA 6 Is Blowing Away Gaming's Greatest Devs, Including Naughty Dog
articles.content_orig:
Naughty Dog’s Michael Barclay – whose credits include Uncharted: The Lost Legacy and The Last of Us 2 – says he’s “made video games for 19 years and GTA 6 appears to me as a Bugatti Veyron would to a nervous Victorian child”.
Rockstar’s latest open world release is by far the best-looking game ever made, even if it is locked to 30fps on PS5 hardware .
And it’s being treated like witchcraft by devs, who naturally have a greater appreciation for the feats on display.
Barclay, who’s currently working on next year’s Intergalactic: The Heretic Prophet , continued :
Subscribe to Push Square on YouTube 172k
“I'm always astonished that [Rockstar’s] environmental lighting is mostly dynamic and looks as good if not better than most baked lighting.”
In really, really simple terms, baked lighting is a game development technique used to save computational cost by calculating light and shadow data in advance.
The downside to this is that it’s fixed, but obviously given the ever-changing nature of GTA 6’s sandbox, it needs to have a dynamic solution.
Barclay is saying that GTA 6’s dynamic lighting matches and even surpasses those pre-determined solutions in many scenarios, making it a real accomplishment.
These comments triggered discussion from various other industry professionals, including Tim Soret from Odd Tales, the makers of The Last Night , who outlined some of his thoughts on the title:
GTA 6 sets a standard so unfathomably high I do wonder at what point it’ll ever be topped.
I suppose raising the bar like this will motivate the many other talented devs around the world, but not every studio will have access to the time and the estimated $1 billion budget that allowed Rockstar to deliver this.
Either way, it’s clear industry professionals are utterly blown away by what the studio has delivered here.

Watch: Trump defends calling Putin a 'friend'
Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelensky has said Vladimir Putin is a "killer" in response to Donald Trump referring to the Russian leader as his "friend" in China this week.
Speaking to CNN, Zelensky said it was up to the US president "how to call Putin" but "for us, he is an enemy... for us, he's a killer".
Before Thursday's historic trilateral meeting with Chinese leader Xi Jinping and Putin, Trump called Putin his "friend" and said the two leaders have had a "great relationship for many years".
Russian attacks continued overnight, with two people killed, including a boy, and 52 injured in missile and drone strikes on Zelensky's hometown of Kryvyi Rih in the central Dnipropetrovsk region, officials said.
Ukraine's state emergency service DSNS said 11 people were also injured in the north-eastern Kharkiv region, and one person in Rivne, in the north-west.
On Friday, at least nine people were killed in Russian strikes targeting bridges in the capital Kyiv and railway stations in western Ukraine - with Zelensky calling the attack the "biggest this year" after an onslaught of 110 missiles, including 27 ballistic, and more than 400 drones.
The strikes came days after Ukraine had badly damaged the Crimean Bridge.
Hours after Friday's strikes on Ukraine, Trump told reporters at the White House that Putin would "love to end the war".
"They [Zelensky and Putin] both want to end it and it's a very good thing I have a relationship," he said on Friday.
Trump also doubled down on his description of the Russian leader as a friend but said he "can't speak" to whether Putin is a friend to the US.
However Zelensky said despite Trump's stance, he saw Putin as "a killer".
"I think mostly for the people in the world, he is a killer because he's killing - by the way- he's killing each day and night," he told CNN.
Zelensky also said speaking about Putin like he was a "friend" meant "he doesn't feel enough pressure".
The war of words came as neighbouring Poland said a Russian cruise missile was among three objects that violated its airspace in the south-east of the country early on Friday.
Polish Defence Minister WÅadysÅaw Kosiniak-Kamysz said the missile hit a rural area at Nowy Lipowiec about 50km (31 miles) from the Ukrainian border.
This was about 100km from where European troops - from 11 of the 36 member nations of the coalition of the willing - were completing a training exercise, Polish authorities said.  Another cruise missile and a jet-powered drone were suspected to have hit two other locations, they added.
On Saturday, Polish Foreign Minister RadosÅaw Sikorski told the BBC the cruise missiles had guidance systems, so "it is very unlikely that they veered off course as a result of Ukrainian electronic warfare".
"This is a war in Europe that affects our security," he told Radio 4's Today programme, also referencing similar incidents in recent months across Europe.
Nobody was hurt and no damage has been reported, but Warsaw described the incident as a "provocation" from Moscow.
Nato Secretary General Mark Rutte condemned "grave violations of Polish airspace" and said the military alliance had scrambled its jets in response.
Russia has made no comment about the violations, which took place during Friday's massive attack on Ukraine.
Putin launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.

articles.title_orig: Fossil fuel dispute threatens to derail COP31 climate deal
articles.title_zh: Fossil fuel dispute threatens to derail COP31 climate deal
articles.content_orig:
Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged in Please refresh your browser to be logged in
Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.
United Nations climate talks in Turkey have approached a final deal as COP31 presidents hope to finally achieve consensus on how to advance the fight against global warming.
COP31 president Murat Kurum told a late-night plenary session: “We believe that we have put forward a text which all the parties can agree upon,” as the conference was set to reconvene on Sunday morning to approve the deal.
To avert the most catastrophic effects of warming, experts warn of the need for urgent and deep cuts to emissions, mainly from the use of coal, oil and gas. The world is already on track to blow past the 2015 Paris Agreement goal of limiting warming to 1.5 degrees Celsius (2.7 degrees Fahrenheit) above pre-industrial temperature.
Civil society organisations wrote to Cop31 ’s joint presidents, Australia’s Chris Bowen and Murat Kurum, overnight to tell them they had hours left to avoid making it “one of the most disappointing Cops [the UN] has ever had”.
“The Global South is being abandoned,” they said. “Developed countries have blocked progress across the negotiations and arrived with no new finance commitments.”
Negotiators ran past a Friday deadline, straight through Saturday and into the early hours of Sunday. Their new version of the deal text refined an earlier draft, which had been heavily criticised by some for lacking ambition because it contained no reference to ending the use of fossil fuels.
Kurum has said he felt concerns around fossil fuels had been addressed, as had those around helping developing countries finance their adaptations to climate change.
Delegations have until 3am GMT to raise any objections to the deal, with a session scheduled at 6am GMT to begin approving it.
Australia led the talks with Turkey, which is hosting the meeting, and nearly 200 delegations from the world’s richest, poorest, largest and smallest nations. It was hoped that a year of climate disasters could help sharpen minds at the conference.
Devastating floods in Mozambique flooded more than 150,000 homes and killed at least 22 people. Coming off the back of other climate disasters in the country - including Cyclone Kenneth in 2019, as well as a crippling drought across 2023 and 2024 - charities told The Independent they were struggling to attract donors due to foreign aid cuts.
In August, after a piece of melting glacier dislodged high up in the mountains, devastating floods in Nepal caused an estimated $4.8bn in damages, and left 1,500 dead and 10,000 injured.
There is also the threat a record breaking El Nino weather event that the UN’s World Food Programme (WFP) has projected that an additional 49 million more people could be pushed into hunger globally.
A climate “loss and damage” fund was established at Cop27 in Egypt in 2022 in order to provide developing countries with compensation for climate disasters. But it has so far secured just $822m in pledges, and countries affected by climate disasters are limited to apply for only $20m per disaster – less than half a per cent of Nepal’s needs.
“Nepal did not create the climate problem. But we keep being hit by massive floods, not just this year but also in 2025, 2022 and other years,” said Bisesh Sangat, a Nepali attendee of Cop31 who works for the NGO Practical Action. “There’s a lot of big infrastructure losses, but also the human losses mean that you go to villages and there are lots of widows and children without fathers, so the losses are very profound.”
There was already deep disappointment after a draft published on Thursday afternoon failed to include any mention of fossil fuels - despite the fact that this had previously been mentioned in the outcome of Cop28 in Dubai in 2023.
This cover decision is seen as the key outcome of the UN climate conference, and is set to be a key signal that countries will take home and implement in national policy.
Mohamed Adow, director of the Power Shift Africa thinktank said: "If this version of the text remains, it will be a ghost COP. The summit will have nothing to show for what happened here. After the progress made in 2023 at Cop28 in Dubai where fossil fuels were mentioned for the first time, there is now no mention of the f-word at all. Cop31 has been muzzled on the most important threat causing the climate crisis."
Stories emerging from the negotiating room suggest that the usual suspects were to blame for an outcome that was less ambitious than hoped. Saudi Arabia has been among the main objectors to any wording on the “transition away from fossil fuels”, with insiders suggesting that the world’s largest oil exporter played a key role in blocking ambitious language.
Pelin Zorlu, senior research fellow lead on climate and energy at the Chatham House think tank, said: “The Cop Presidency has acknowledged the difficulty of reaching consensus on fossil fuels, with opposition from the Arab Group, Russia and others.”
But others pointed their fingers at the EU for not being ambitious enough, particularly around Turkey’s high profile pledge to raise electricity's share of total final energy consumption from around 23 per cent today to 35 per cent by 2035. Such a move makes sense if the electricity is powered by renewables – but not if it is done so with coal.
Laurie van der Burg, from NGO Oil Change International, said: “The EU is trying to shift blame onto others and it is deeply hypocritical. At the beginning of Cop31, it signalled it was prepared to drop the renewable energy sources ask from the electrification target and it has failed to put forward an EU fossil fuel transition roadmap. Even worse, the EU blocked progress on the public finance, adaptation, and just transition that developing countries urgently need. These are not side issues. They are essential to making a fair fossil fuel phaseout possible and protecting communities from climate disasters.”
At the same time, the EU and other wealthy democracies have expressed dismay at receiving too much blame when it is they who are providing the bulk of climate finance - and especially so with the US absent. EU member states provided €32.3bn in public “climate finance” in 2025, which mobilised a further €9.3bn in private finance.
There is growing disquiet that the group of countries who are required to provide this “climate finance” – crucial capital needed to decarbonise and adapt to climate change – is fixed around a list of developed countries that was devised in 1992, known as “Annex II”. It means that newly-wealthy countries, including China, the UAE, South Korea and Singapore, do not officially have to provide climate finance, while the likes of Greece and Portugal are required to.
While plenty of lobbyists were in attendance, one group was conspicuously absent: world leaders. Neither China’s Xi Jinping or India’s Narendra Modi, or any hint of the US federal government made an appearance – with Andy Burnham the only G7 leader in attendance. Yet, while powerful countries fight it out, ultimately it is the world’s most climate vulnerable countries who are losing out.
On Friday afternoon, Ghana's minister for environment, science and technology, Dr Zanetor Agyeman-Rawlings did not mince her words.
Africans were being “excluded by the use of technicalities, with the use of inaccessible finance, and with the use of shifting goalposts and lack of commitment and delivery on promises… Africa is not a continent merely seeking assistance. We are asking the developed countries to keep promises that they already made.”
In what seemed to be a reference to the US, she said: “There are countries who from the onset decided not to be a part of this agreement. There, they were plain and honest… What we do not appreciate are those who choose to remain a part of the framewor

articles.title_orig: These iPhone Customizations Can Make Your Lock Screen Look Cooler
articles.title_zh: These iPhone Customizations Can Make Your Lock Screen Look Cooler
articles.content_orig:
Over the past few years, Apple has improved how much users can customize their iPhone Lock Screen. Initially, the company only allowed changes to the background wallpaper. Then, how it showed wallpaper when the screen dimmed. Now, the lock screen works with customization widgets, allowing you to add and change many aspects of what the iPhone's Lock Screen can do . You could tweak the clock, the wallpaper, fonts, and add color filters. Suddenly, there were widgets and Live Activities too. The latest iOS 27 update, which comes with the all-new Siri AI, also included more customizations to the clock and widgets, allowing you to make the iPhone look more your own.
Interestingly enough, Apple's great revamp on iPhone customization started with iOS 18 , which coincides with the moment the company should've made available all the Apple Intelligence features we are only seeing now. The company had already begun offering ways to change the lock screen with widgets, filters, and new fonts. With iOS 18, Apple added those features to the Home Screen, and Control Center, while making more refinements to the lock screen too.
After that, Apple brought the Liquid Glass design language with iOS 26, which gave the iPhone's software a visual overhaul. As of 2026, Apple's included improvements like animated album covers from Apple Music on the Lock Screen, access to up to three Live Activities in the Dynamic Island, and more.
All that change is a lot to keep track of. So here's an easy list of the best ways you can customize your iPhone Lock Screen to look cooler.
If you're running iOS 27 and have access to the new set of Apple Intelligence features thanks to the new Siri AI, one of the coolest things you can do is to extend your wallpaper on the Lock Screen. For example, if you have the perfect photo, but it's in landscape orientation, or you don't want your partner's or pet's face too zoomed in on your Lock Screen, here's what you can do: After long pressing the Lock Screen > Adding/Customizing a Lock Screen , you can zoom out the image until the iPhone gets an "Extend" feature. Using on-device AI, the iPhone will recreate a part of the image to make it fit the vibe you're going for.
Once you do that, you can customize other parts of your Lock Screen. If you have an iPhone with the Action Button and Camera Control functionalities, for example, you can remove the traditional Flashlight and Camera widgets to something else you might want to access faster, if these options are redundant to you. There's a number of shortcuts you can choose from, including Apple options and third-party apps. Et voilà, you have the most original Lock Screen possible.
Another cool feature introduced with iOS 27 is the opposite of what previous software brought. While the Lock Screen clock was getting bigger over the years, now you can make it smaller to give it a very minimal aesthetic look. Just tap on the clock while editing, and then on the upper right of the font options is a button that looks like two rectangles. Tap it, and your clock will shrink into the date area.
Another important tweak that few people actually take advantage of is Apple's Focus Modes. Introduced in 2021's iOS 15 update , Apple lets you create different Lock Screen, Home Screen, wallpapers, and filters for different parts of your day or mood. You can create one for work, and another for while you're in the car. If you're at swim practice, you can set another wallpaper and only allow specific people to call you, etc.
Mastering Focus Mode can take a while because it has so many potential combinations of its features, but the outcome can be very rewarding. Many people use it to avoid getting those endless social media notifications during work hours, or even prevent Trello and Slack from buzzing you when you're long gone from your work. Did I mention these Focus Modes can be set up by location? Since your phone knows where you are, the Focus Modes can trigger when you get to or leave a specific place, by a specific hour, or even when Apple Intelligence understands you're doing something else — like when you start playing a game or commuting on the bus.
You can find Focus Modes by opening the Control Center and venturing inside the Focus tab. With that, you can go beyond the Do Not Disturb option and create different filters for the day, including unique Lock Screen combinations that make sense for that specific moment of the day.
Another cool feature for someone who wants a completely different Lock Screen wallpaper is to create AI-generated wallpapers based on your photos, or memoji, or even just a prompt you give about a visual you're imagining in your head. When customizing a Lock Screen , tap the Plus button , then Image Playground , select between a few design styles, and then describe an image for a unique wallpaper. A bonus tip is that with iOS 27, you can even remove the Now Playing card from the Lock Screen, and whatever is playing will continue to play, bringing the ultimate minimalist design.

articles.title_orig: Trump opens door to bipartisan deal on credit card rates as Americans face record debt
articles.title_zh: Trump opens door to bipartisan deal on credit card rates as Americans face record debt
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
NEW YORK (AP) — President Donald Trump said Saturday that he would work with the incoming Democratic Congress to cap credit card interest rates , hoping to fulfill a promise he made on the 2024 campaign trail but couldn't deliver on because of industry pressure and a lack of interest from his fellow Republicans.
"I would do it. These credit card companies have made a lot," Trump told Fox News Channel's "Saturday in America."
Democrats and the Republican president have both backed capping credit card interest rates, with the standard proposal being capping rates at 10%. It would substantially reduce what credit card companies can charge customers . The median credit card interest rate is roughly 22.2%, according to an August survey by the New York Federal Reserve.
Trump proposed capping credit card interest rates in January, as part of the White House's affordability push . Banks and credit card companies immediately and aggressively opposed the proposal, saying any interest rate cap would force them to cancel cards for the poor and less creditworthy customers or substantially cut back on the rewards they offer when customers spend on their cards.
The proposal also did not sit well with Republicans, and there was little effort by the GOP-controlled Congress to fulfill Trump's promise.
That could change now that Democrats will control both the House and Senate. Sen. Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass., who is expected to be the next chair of the Senate Banking Committee, has said repeatedly she wants to cap rates.
In response to the Fox News interview, Warren said: "Let's cap credit card interest rates and save Americans money."
Other Democrats have endorsed the idea in various ways, including Rep. Maxine Waters of California, a powerful Democrat who sits on the House Financial Services Committee. Among Republicans, Sen. Josh Hawley of Missouri has proposed several caps on credit card interest rates, as recently as this year when Trump made his proposal.
"The President is right. Let's pass my bill to cap credit card interest fees," Hawley posted on X on Saturday.
Researchers who studied Trump's campaign pledge after it was first announced found that Americans would save roughly $100 billion in interest a year if credit card rates were capped at 10%. The same researchers found that while the credit card industry would take a major hit, it would still be profitable, although credit card rewards and other perks might be scaled back.
About 195 million people in the United States had credit cards in 2024 and were assessed $160 billion in interest charges, the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau says.
Americans are now carrying more credit card debt than ever, to the tune of about $1.23 trillion, according to figures from the New York Federal Reserve for the third quarter last year.

articles.title_orig: UN climate talk negotiators go into second day of overtime while at odds over fossil fuels
articles.title_zh: UN climate talk negotiators go into second day of overtime while at odds over fossil fuels
articles.content_orig:
Talks were set to resume at the UN COP31 summit on Sunday for a second day of overtime as countries struggle to reach a new global climate deal.
Nations were deadlocked in Turkey on how to advance the fight against global warming, after new draft agreements included no reference to reducing the world's demand for fossil fuels.
A third and "final" text was sent to delegates in the early hours of Sunday morning and members had until 06:00 local time (0300 GMT) to raise concerns before a 9am local time (0600GMT) meeting for approval.
If countries cannot reach consensus - as required by the UN's climate talks process - the negotiations could be suspended to reconvene next year.
A draft deal unveiled earlier this week called for a faster phase-out of fossil fuels, but a second, pared-down version released Thursday stripped away all mentions of coal, oil and gas - sparking threats of a walk out.
The fallout led to the summit in Antalya blowing past the original deadline of Friday . On Saturday negotiating teams who had Sunday morning flights were rescheduling them - a sign a deal was still not in sight, and raising the risk that as teams eventually had to leave, the meeting could lose the critical numbers needed to pass an agreement.
As part of a last ditch effort to produce an acceptable text, the European Union and Saudi Arabia - who were deeply divided over the future of fossil fuels - were brought together on Saturday to seek a compromise.
COP31 President and Turkish Environment Minister Murat Kurum told delegates in the early hours of Sunday morning he believed concerns had been addressed.
"We ask you to look at this decision carefully," Kurum said.
"We are closer than ever to agreement on the remaining issues."
If the countries can't agree, the summit would end with no deal and be reconvened next year.
This has only happened once before since countries started holding COP climate meetings in 1995.
Ministers from Panama, Solomon Islands, Cote d'Ivoire and the EU were fighting to have a commitment to move away from fossil fuels put back into the final agreement, after fossil fuel producers led by Saudi Arabia pushed for its removal.
"It is not acceptable to have a COP or a cover decision that does not even mention fossil fuels and we simply will not put up with it," said Juan Carlos Navarro, Panama's minister for the environment.
Tuvalu's Climate Minister Maina Talia told reporters it was a "red line" for the low-lying Pacific nation: "We're talking about the root cause of all of this".
France's Minister of Ecological Transition, Monique Barbut, took aim at several references in the text to carbon capture - a technology that takes emissions when they are released and stores them underground.
She said it was being used as a licence for other countries to keep burning oil and gas.
"We cannot be announcing to the world that we are now getting to 1.5 increase in the temperature and do business like nothing was happening," Barbut said.
For the first time at a COP, the agreement - known officially as the Antalya Accords - could acknowledge that the goal set under the Paris climate accord of keeping global temperature rise below 1.5C has been missed.
The world is entering a period called "overshoot".
Beyond this point scientists warn millions more people will be exposed to sea level rise and extreme heat.
But Australia's Climate Change and Energy Minister, Chris Bowen, who is leading negotiations, pushed back on the need to include language on fossil fuels.
He argued the summit was about implementation, and should focus on the move towards clean energy sources.
Another key issues raised by developing nations is the the lack of money.
Another sticking point involved a push from the Africa Group to get commitments on more money for adaptations to climate change, however the EU has previously said it would not support this.
Earlier versions of the text included an agreement to ramp up money for adaptation to $120bn (£91bn) by 2035 - a figure that was then removed.
"We did not come here to beg, we came here to claim what is rightfully ours for our people who are suffering the brunt of anthropogenic activities of developed countries," said Zanetor Agyeman Rawlings, Ghana's Environment Minister and chair of the African Group of negotiators.
Climate activists and environmental groups, who are observers to these talks, have slammed negotiations.
"I can tell you without any doubt that this has been the worst COP ever," said Mohamed Adow of Powershift Africa.

articles.title_orig: Motorola Moto Tag 3 listed on Amazon - GSMArena.com news
articles.title_zh: Motorola Moto Tag 3 listed on Amazon - GSMArena.com news
articles.content_orig:
Motorola Accessories Rumors
Motorola unveiled the Moto Tag in 2024 and followed up with the Moto Tag 2 in January this year. Considering the gap between the first and second-gen Moto Tags, we weren't expecting Motorola to launch Moto Tag 3 anytime soon, but it seems Motorola could launch it in a few months, or even weeks, as it is already listed on Amazon.
Amazon UK has listed the Moto Tag in Pantone Lucent White color, while Amazon Italy has listed the Pantone Indigo Blue version. If both listings are to be believed, the Moto Tag 3 will be hardly different from the Moto Tag 2, as it looks identical and shares the same features.
Motorola Moto Tag 3 in Pantone Lucent White color
Like the Moto Tag 2, the Moto Tag 3 uses Ultra-Wideband (UWB) and Bluetooth technology, has an IP68 rating, weighs 8.5 g, and is fueled by a replaceable CR2032 battery.
Amazon states the CR2032 cell will provide more than 500 days of battery life on the Moto Tag 3, which is the same as the Moto Tag 2 . However, Motorola's US and UK websites list the Moto Tag 2 as having more than 600 days of battery life.
Motorola Moto Tag 3 in Pantone Indigo Blue
Here's what Amazon's product description for the Moto Tag 3 reads: “Motorola moto tag 3 helps you locate everyday items with precision and reliability. Using Ultra Wideband and Bluetooth technology, it works with the Android Find Hub network to track belongings both nearby and at distance. With more than 500 days of battery life powered by a replaceable CR2032 battery, it is designed for long-term use. Built-in privacy protections, encrypted location data, and unwanted tracking alerts support secure tracking in a compact, IP68-rated design suitable for daily carry.”
The model number mentioned in the Moto Tag 3 images on Amazon is XT2561-1. It is the same as the Moto Tag 2, which makes us wonder whether we're really looking at the new Moto Tag 3 or just new colors for the Moto Tag 2 listed under the wrong name. The Moto Tag 2 is currently available in Pantone Arabesque and Pantone Laurel Oak.

articles.title_orig: Intel Nova Lake-H Spec Sheet Shows Up With a 4.8 GHz Boost and 25 W TDP
articles.title_zh: Intel Nova Lake-H Spec Sheet Shows Up With a 4.8 GHz Boost and 25 W TDP
articles.content_orig:
We finally got a glimpse of one of the upcoming 16-core Nova Lake mobile chip, and what it brings to the table.
Here is one of the early appearances of one of the upcoming Intel Core Ultra 4 series processors. Thanks to @momomo_us, we got a glimpse of a Nova Lake-H mobile processor on an Advantech board (for robotics and industrial applications), which is going to power the next-gen mainstream mobile devices. The specs sheet doesn't mention the SKU model name, but it mentions "Core Ultra Series 4" and "Nova Lake-H" as the codename.
The specs sheet details most of its specifications, including the core configuration, cache size, memory support, and TDP rating. The processor uses an 8P+4E+4LPE configuration, combining eight performance cores, four efficient cores, and four low-power efficient cores. Even though this is the same configuration as the 16-core Nova Lake-S processor we reported on previously , this one is specifically for the mobile platform.
The processor is expected to carry the Coyote Cove architecture for the P cores and Arctic Wolf E cores as previously reported. The 16-core Nova Lake-H leaked SKU is reportedly featuring a good 4.8 GHz Turbo clock, 2.0 GHz base clock, and 18 MB of LLC cache. The page also mentions its integrated graphics configuration, which reportedly features a 2.3 GHz clock speed. However, details like execution units and architecture are missing.
It's expected that the Nova Lake-H SKUs will have integrated Arc graphics based on the Xe3P architecture and will carry up to 12 GPU cores for the higher-end variants. This might be the one that carries the 12-GPU-core configuration, but we will wait for official confirmation. One more interesting detail here is the memory support. The processor reportedly supports DDR5-8000 MT/s and up to 128 GB of capacity. This aligns with our previous reports that suggested a good 800 MT/s jump over Panther Lake, which supports DDR5-7200 MT/s.
Another key detail is the power rating, as the leaked specs reveal the SKU reportedly runs at a 25W TDP. This is well below the power range expected from the Nova Lake-S desktop processors, for which vendors have started introducing PSUs with three 8-pin EPS connectors .
The leaker @momomo_us also spotted a Nova Lake-S listing on the OpenBenchmarking platform. This is an early Nova Lake-S sample with 28 Cores and up to 5.2 GHz turbo boost. This is likely the 8P+16E+4LP-E configuration chip that could carry a 296W PL2 limit .

articles.title_orig: The Penny Is Dead. Now It’s Official.
articles.title_zh: The Penny Is Dead. Now It’s Official.
articles.content_orig:
President Trump on Friday signed the Common Cents Act , which lets businesses round cash transactions to the nearest nickel, into law.
It sets standards for cash transactions that businesses and consumers can use when exact change isn't available, as the penny is phased out. The legislation calls for cash transactions to be rounded up or down to the nearest 5 cents. For example, if a purchase costs $10.02 after tax and a customer is short 2 cents, the tab would round down to $10 under the act. A charge of $10.04 would round up to $10.05.
Before its passage, businesses could be sued if they failed to give customers exact change, even when rounding up in a patron's favor.
Business advocacy groups cheered its passage. NACS, which represents the convenience and fuel retailing industry, said it creates reliable guidelines for conducting cash transactions.
"Retailers have been looking for federal guidance on processing cash transactions since penny production ended," Brennan Duckett, NACS' director of regulatory and policy, said in a statement to CBS News. "NACS members benefit directly from this law, and we are pleased to see President Trump make it official with his signature."
Business owners said they faced confusion and were vulnerable to litigation before the act passed.
"As a retailer, I am grateful to have established legal guidance on rounding cash transactions," Scott Zietlow, CEO and president of Kwik Trip, said in a statement Friday. "Every cash transaction that we processed in recent months was a reminder that we needed more clarity from the federal government. We've now got that clarity."
